27	
28	| File | Round-1 verdict | Status now | Evidence (with page) | Exact remaining correction |
29	|---|---|---|---|---|
30	| `principle--concentration-of-training-workloads.md` | FIX | **NEW PROBLEM** [major] | (1) The Contested paragraph says the 2008 "does not work well for high-performance athletes" claim (PDF 19 / p.8, verified) "is disputed by Issurin's own later peer-reviewed review", which "judges concentrated-unidirectional block programs' evidence insufficient". That finding is about Verkhoshansky's CU model (Issurin 2016 pp.6-7, Table 1 "based on Verkhoshansky"). The same review supports multi-targeted BP with 28 studies and restates the critique of the traditional model (p.6, p.11); see the section above. (2) The Eric's-baseline sentence is garbled: "...not as an independent convergence: "you can't ride two horses with one saddle", incompatible qualities are not both trained...". Checked and fixed: link to `[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]` works; Table 1.4 "There is sufficient energy supply" locator note matches idx 20; Fig 1.7 quotes (idx 37); low/mid carve-out (idx 44); Bompa 1984 (idx 13); Bompa inference relabelled; week1-lecture.md lines 1795 and 1838 confirm the Issurin attribution and "Can't ride 2 horses". | Replace the whole Contested paragraph with: "**Contested (Issurin 2008 vs Issurin 2016):** this book limits the concentration principle to high-level athletes, saying medium-level concentration 'still provides sufficient stimulation' for low- and mid-level athletes (PDF 44 / p.33). Issurin's later review says 'proper analysis gives no evidence that amateur athletes have any serious restrictions when implementing highly concentrated workloads structured in blocks of optimal duration' (Issurin 2016, p.11, `research-papers/issurin-2016-...`). The same review restricts only Verkhoshansky's concentrated-unidirectional model, where many interacting abilities are needed (pp.6-7). The Contested paragraph cites Issurin 2016 p.6 (team and combat CU studies with no game data) as "a direct qualification of the confident five-benefit list above". The problems are in what three of them are cited *for* (rows below).

## Read this first: round 1 was wrong about Issurin 2016 (do not re-apply its correction)

Round 1 told the fixer to re-ground `contested` in the principle and training-stage entries on the vault brief for Issurin (2016). The brief says concentrated-unidirectional evidence was "insufficient" for combat, team-sport and swimming preparation [its p.6] and "restricted when peak performance requires many interacting abilities" [its p.11]. The fixer applied this exactly. **The correction was itself wrong.** The original paper shows:

- The "concentrated unidirectional (CU)" model is **Verkhoshansky's**, not Issurin's. Table 1 is "based on Verkhoshansky [9, 10]". The p.6 findings (basketball, handball and soccer fitness gains with no game data; swimmers 2 of 3) all come from Table 2, "Effects of concentrated unidirectional bloc periodization training programs".
- Issurin's own A-T-R model is the **multi-targeted BP** version. Section 3 starts at p.7, and p.11 names the canoe-kayak, track and swimming lineage. The review reports it is "supported by the findings of 28 studies" [p.11].
- The review does not soften the 2008 critique of the traditional model; it repeats it. CU "has no advantage over traditional planning, because it does not allow the multi-peak annual design" [p.6]. The conclusion also reads: "It would be a regrettable mistake to think that the traditional theory of training should stay the same" [p.11].

So the 2016 review cannot "dispute" the 2008 line "does not work well for high-performance athletes". Both entries now misstate a library source.

**There is a real Issurin-vs-Issurin contradiction to use instead.** It sits on the principle entry's own When NOT carve-out:

- 2008 (PDF 44 / p.33): the traditional approach "has visible benefits for the preparation of low- and mid-level athletes ... medium-level concentration still provides sufficient stimulation".
- 2016 [p.11]: "proper analysis gives no evidence that amateur athletes have any serious restrictions when implementing highly concentrated workloads structured in blocks of optimal duration". It also cites a recreational-trainee study where the block program was "considerably superior".

**Upstream note (the fixer cannot act on it; flag to Eric):** the vault brief `research-papers/issurin-2016-...md` never says that "concentrated-unidirectional" means Verkhoshansky's model, which is why this misreading happened. 18	
19	# Issurin 2016 — Benefits and limitations of block-periodized preparation
20	
21	> **Citation**
22	> Issurin, V. B. (2016). Benefits and limitations of block periodized training approaches to athletes' preparation: A review. *Sports Medicine, 46*(3), 329–338. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-015-0425-5
23	
24	## Why it was promoted
25	
26	This review distinguishes concentrated-unidirectional and multi-targeted block models and provides a useful conceptual vocabulary for discussing concentrated workloads and sequencing.
27	
28	## Research question
29	
30	What benefits, limitations, and sport-context boundaries are reported for two versions of block-periodized athlete preparation?
31	
32	## Population and context
33	
34	- The review emphasizes elite, subelite, and well-trained athletes across endurance, team, combat, dual, jumping, and strength/power settings. [p. 11]
35	- It also discusses a smaller number of recreational-athlete studies.
36	- It is a training-theory review, not evidence specific to collegiate American football.
37	
38	## Study design and methods
39	
40	- Narrative review contrasting concentrated-unidirectional and multi-targeted block-periodization models.
41	- The article summarizes prior studies in tables but does not report a systematic search, eligibility process, formal risk-of-bias appraisal, or meta-analysis.
42	- Consequently, the stated number and direction of supportive studies should be interpreted as an author-curated synthesis rather than a pooled comparative estimate.
43	
44	## Key findings
45	
46	- Concentrated-unidirectional programs in combat and team sports improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team practice or competitive performance. [p. 6]
47	- In an elite-swimmer example, specific strength and anaerobic capacity improved but swimming performance improved in only two of three athletes. [p. 6]
48	- The author judged the concentrated-unidirectional evidence insufficient for broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation. [p. 6]
49	- The review reports support from 28 studies for multi-targeted block programs, but the designs, populations, outcomes, and comparator quality varied. [p. 11]
50	- The concentrated-unidirectional model was presented as better suited to sports dominated by a narrow target quality and as restricted when peak performance requires many interacting abilities. [p. 11]
51	
52	## Limitations and applicability
53	
54	- Non-systematic study selection and absent risk-of-bias assessment create a substantial risk of selective emphasis.
55	- Fitness improvements are not interchangeable with sport-specific performance, availability, or competitive outcomes. [p. 6]
56	- Training models were not consistently isolated from total volume, intensity, exercise choice, coaching, or athlete history.
57	- Evidence spans dissimilar sports and training levels; it does not supply validated block durations or effect estimates for collegiate American football.
58	- The strong conclusion favoring multi-targeted block periodization is the author's synthesis and should not be treated as settled comparative evidence. [p. 11]
59	
60	## Practitioner interpretation
61	
62	Use block periodization as a planning hypothesis: concentrate compatible emphases when competition structure and athlete needs justify it, while maintaining the qualities and technical exposure that cannot safely decay. Judge the plan by sport-specific performance, availability, and individual response—not by the periodization label. Compare it prospectively with the program's own prior practice where feasible.
63	
64	## Evidence map
65	
66	| Claim | Locator | Evidence type |
67	|---|---|---|
68	| Review scope and distinction between two models | p. 4 | narrative framing |
69	| Concentrated-unidirectional evidence and performance gaps | p. 6 | narrative synthesis |
70	| Multi-targeted evidence claim and applicability boundaries | p. 11 | narrative synthesis/limitation |
71

# Issurin 2016 — Benefits and limitations of block-periodized preparation

> **Citation**
> Issurin, V. B. (2016). Benefits and limitations of block periodized training approaches to athletes' preparation: A review. *Sports Medicine, 46*(3), 329–338. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-015-0425-5

## Why it was promoted

This review distinguishes concentrated-unidirectional and multi-targeted block models and provides a useful conceptual vocabulary for discussing concentrated workloads and sequencing.

## Research question

What benefits, limitations, and sport-context boundaries are reported for two versions of block-periodized athlete preparation?

## Population and context

- The review emphasizes elite, subelite, and well-trained athletes across endurance, team, combat, dual, jumping, and strength/power settings. [p. 11]
- It also discusses a smaller number of recreational-athlete studies.
- It is a training-theory review, not evidence specific to collegiate American football.

## Study design and methods

- Narrative review contrasting concentrated-unidirectional and multi-targeted block-periodization models.
- The article summarizes prior studies in tables but does not report a systematic search, eligibility process, formal risk-of-bias appraisal, or meta-analysis.
- Consequently, the stated number and direction of supportive studies should be interpreted as an author-curated synthesis rather than a pooled comparative estimate.

## Key findings

- Concentrated-unidirectional programs in combat and team sports improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team practice or competitive performance. [p. 6]
- In an elite-swimmer example, specific strength and anaerobic capacity improved but swimming performance improved in only two of three athletes. [p. 6]
- The author judged the concentrated-unidirectional evidence insufficient for broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation. [p. 6]
- The review reports support from 28 studies for multi-targeted block programs, but the designs, populations, outcomes, and comparator quality varied. [p. 11]
- The concentrated-unidirectional model was presented as better suited to sports dominated by a narrow target quality and as restricted when peak performance requires many interacting abilities. [p. 11]

## Limitations and applicability

- Non-systematic study selection and absent risk-of-bias assessment create a substantial risk of selective emphasis.
- Fitness improvements are not interchangeable with sport-specific performance, availability, or competitive outcomes. [p. 6]
- Training models were not consistently isolated from total volume, intensity, exercise choice, coaching, or athlete history.
- Evidence spans dissimilar sports and training levels; it does not supply validated block durations or effect estimates for collegiate American football.
- The strong conclusion favoring multi-targeted block periodization is the author's synthesis and should not be treated as settled comparative evidence. [p. 11]

## Practitioner interpretation

Use block periodization as a planning hypothesis: concentrate compatible emphases when competition structure and athlete needs justify it, while maintaining the qualities and technical exposure that cannot safely decay. Judge the plan by sport-specific performance, availability, and individual response—not by the periodization label. Compare it prospectively with the program's own prior practice where feasible.

## Evidence map

| Claim | Locator | Evidence type |
|---|---|---|
| Review scope and distinction between two models | p. 4 | narrative framing |
| Concentrated-unidirectional evidence and performance gaps | p. 6 | narrative synthesis |
| Multi-targeted evidence claim and applicability boundaries | p. 11 | narrative synthesis/limitation |

# Comyns & Flanagan 2013 — Applying session RPE in professional rugby union

> **Citation**
> Comyns, T., & Flanagan, E. P. (2013). Applications of the session rating of perceived exertion system in professional rugby union. *Strength & Conditioning Journal, 35*(6), 78–85. https://doi.org/10.1519/SSC.0000000000000015

## Why it was promoted

This applied article gives a clear implementation model for session RPE in professional rugby union, including calculation, weekly visualization, return-to-training use, and common data-collection errors.

## Research question

How can professional rugby union practitioners calculate and use session RPE, weekly training load, monotony, and strain to manage squad and individual training?

## Population and context

- Participants: No prospectively recruited sample; examples and observations come from the authors' applied work with two professional rugby teams.
- Sport and level: Professional rugby union.
- Training or return-to-play context: Preseason and in-season squad planning, taper weeks, acute-injury return to full training, and chronic-injury load management.
- Inclusion and exclusion boundaries: The 24-week squad example included only a "fit to play" group completing all modalities; injured or adapted-plan players were excluded from squad averages.

## Study design and methods

- Design: Practitioner tutorial and narrative synthesis with descriptive examples, not a controlled intervention or formal validation study.
- Exposure or intervention: Session RPE monitoring across rugby, strength, speed, conditioning, and competition.
- Comparator: Planned versus perceived load patterns, between-week trends, and individual trends relative to a fit-to-play squad average.
- Measurements and outcomes: Global CR-10 session RPE collected 30 minutes after training; session load equals RPE multiplied by session duration; weekly load, monotony, and strain are derived from daily values. [p. 3]
- Analysis: Descriptive calculations and visualizations from applied professional-rugby data; no inferential analysis of the displayed team examples is reported.

## Key findings

- The authors' professional-rugby example accumulated average weekly loads of 2,400–2,600 AU in early preseason and approximately 1,800–1,900 AU in season, including match load. [p. 4]
- In the within-week examples, two schedules with the same absolute weekly load of 2,125 AU produced different strain; the more homogeneous schedule increased strain by approximately 30%. [p. 5]
- In planned download weeks, athletes typically accumulated 70–80% of the training load from other weeks in the same block, according to the authors' applied observations. [p. 6]
- The authors recommend recording nontraining days as zero load because omitting zeros artificially inflates calculated monotony and strain. [p. 8]

## Limitations and applicability

- The article is instructional and largely experience-based; the displayed rugby examples do not report sample size, uncertainty, hypothesis tests, or injury/performance outcomes.
- Session RPE is subjective, and stable "high raters" make absolute values unsuitable for direct player-to-player comparison; the authors favor comparing each player's trend with the squad trend. [p. 8]
- Results and thresholds from two professional rugby settings should not be treated as universal targets for other teams, competitive levels, sports, or individuals.
- Timing conventions, warm-up inclusion, actual versus scheduled match duration, rest-day zeros, and fit-to-play roster definitions must remain consistent to preserve longitudinal meaning. [pp. 7-8]
- The authors conclude that session RPE should complement, rather than replace, external-load and objective internal-load monitoring. [p. 8]

## Practitioner interpretation

Use session RPE as a low-cost longitudinal layer that integrates the athlete's perceived internal load across training modalities. Define collection and duration rules before the season, audit missing rest-day zeros, and interpret individual trends rather than borrowing the article's absolute AU values as prescriptions. In Baylor American-football work, this rugby-union example may inform workflow design but requires sport-, position-, and schedule-specific calibration.

## Evidence map

| Claim | Locator | Evidence type |
|---|---|---|
| Session RPE calculation and derived weekly metrics | p. 3 | method |
| Professional-rugby preseason and in-season examples | p. 4 | descriptive result |
| Same weekly load but different strain by organization | p. 5 | descriptive result |
| Download-week observations | p. 6 | descriptive result |
| Collection errors and interpretation limits | pp. 7-8 | limitation |
| Complementary role of session RPE | p. 8 | conclusion |

21	> **Citation**
22	> McLaren, S. J., Smith, A., Spears, I. R., & Weston, M. (2017). A detailed quantification of differential ratings of perceived exertion during team-sport training. *Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport, 20*(3), 290–295. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsams.2016.06.011
23	
24	## Why it was promoted
25	
26	This paper informs whether a single global session-RPE score hides meaningful differences in respiratory, lower-limb, upper-body, and cognitive/technical exertion.
27	
28	## Research question
29	
30	Do differential session-RPE measures distinguish the perceptual demands of common team-sport training modes, and how do those dimensions relate to global session-RPE load?
31	
32	## Population and context
33	
34	- Participants: 29 professional male rugby-union players (14 forwards, 15 backs), age 24 ± 3 years.
35	- Sport and level: One English Rugby Football Union Championship club.
36	- Training or return-to-play context: Six-week preparatory training period.
37	- Inclusion and exclusion boundaries: One male professional squad; observational training data without standardized experimental external loads.
38	
39	## Study design and methods
40	
41	- Design: Prospective observational longitudinal cohort.
42	- Exposure or intervention: Seven normal training modes across a six-week preparatory block.
43	- Comparator: High-intensity intervals, repeated high-intensity efforts, speed, skill conditioning, skills, whole-body resistance, and upper-body resistance.
44	- Measurements and outcomes: CR100 global session RPE plus breathlessness, leg, upper-body, and cognitive/technical differential RPE; each multiplied by duration.
45	- Analysis: Mixed linear models and multiple regression with magnitude-based interpretation.
46	
47	## Key findings
48	
49	- Differential-RPE models explained 66% to 91% of variance in global session-RPE load across training modes. [Table 2, p. 5]
50	- The strongest dimension varied by mode: leg exertion for high-intensity intervals (r = 0.67, 90% CL ±0.22), breathlessness for repeated high-intensity efforts (r = 0.89, ±0.08), cognitive/technical demand for speed (r = 0.63, ±0.17), and upper-body exertion for upper-body resistance training (r = 0.92, ±0.07). [Table 2, p. 5]
51	- The authors concluded that training modes elicited distinct perceptual profiles that a single score may not fully represent. [pp. 4–5]
52	
53	## Limitations and applicability
54	
55	- External load was not quantified as part of this study, limiting inference about why perceptual dimensions differed. [p. 4]
56	- Ratings were collected 15–30 minutes post-session, and the authors acknowledged a possible latency effect. [p. 2]

58	- Practitioner transfer limitation: Associations with global RPE do not validate differential RPE as an injury predictor or prescribe universal response thresholds.

60	## Practitioner interpretation
61	
62	Differential RPE can be added when the program needs to distinguish central, lower-limb, upper-body, or cognitive stress. Use athlete-specific trends to clarify the source of a high global load, while retaining the session plan and external-load context.

# McLaren et al. 2017 — Differential RPE across team-sport training modes

> **Citation**
> McLaren, S. J., Smith, A., Spears, I. R., & Weston, M. (2017). A detailed quantification of differential ratings of perceived exertion during team-sport training. *Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport, 20*(3), 290–295. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsams.2016.06.011

## Why it was promoted

This paper informs whether a single global session-RPE score hides meaningful differences in respiratory, lower-limb, upper-body, and cognitive/technical exertion.

## Research question

Do differential session-RPE measures distinguish the perceptual demands of common team-sport training modes, and how do those dimensions relate to global session-RPE load?

## Population and context

- Participants: 29 professional male rugby-union players (14 forwards, 15 backs), age 24 ± 3 years.
- Sport and level: One English Rugby Football Union Championship club.
- Training or return-to-play context: Six-week preparatory training period.
- Inclusion and exclusion boundaries: One male professional squad; observational training data without standardized experimental external loads.

## Study design and methods

- Design: Prospective observational longitudinal cohort.
- Exposure or intervention: Seven normal training modes across a six-week preparatory block.
- Comparator: High-intensity intervals, repeated high-intensity efforts, speed, skill conditioning, skills, whole-body resistance, and upper-body resistance.
- Measurements and outcomes: CR100 global session RPE plus breathlessness, leg, upper-body, and cognitive/technical differential RPE; each multiplied by duration.
- Analysis: Mixed linear models and multiple regression with magnitude-based interpretation.

## Key findings

- Differential-RPE models explained 66% to 91% of variance in global session-RPE load across training modes. [Table 2, p. 5]
- The strongest dimension varied by mode: leg exertion for high-intensity intervals (r = 0.67, 90% CL ±0.22), breathlessness for repeated high-intensity efforts (r = 0.89, ±0.08), cognitive/technical demand for speed (r = 0.63, ±0.17), and upper-body exertion for upper-body resistance training (r = 0.92, ±0.07). [Table 2, p. 5]
- The authors concluded that training modes elicited distinct perceptual profiles that a single score may not fully represent. [pp. 4–5]

## Limitations and applicability

- External load was not quantified as part of this study, limiting inference about why perceptual dimensions differed. [p. 4]
- Ratings were collected 15–30 minutes post-session, and the authors acknowledged a possible latency effect. [p. 2]
- The paper labels specific training substitutions as speculative and calls for further research. [p. 6]
- Practitioner transfer limitation: Associations with global RPE do not validate differential RPE as an injury predictor or prescribe universal response thresholds.

## Practitioner interpretation

Differential RPE can be added when the program needs to distinguish central, lower-limb, upper-body, or cognitive stress. Use athlete-specific trends to clarify the source of a high global load, while retaining the session plan and external-load context.

## Evidence map

| Claim | Locator | Evidence type |
|---|---|---|
| Sample, six-week design, and training modes | p. 2 | method |
| Mode-specific regression results | Table 2, p. 5 | result |
| Post-session latency caveat | p. 2 | limitation |
| Speculative programming recommendations | p. 6 | limitation |

## Related knowledge

- [[session-rpe]] — global internal load
- [[differential-rpe]] — perceptual load dimensions
- [[rugby-union-training-load]] — applied population

It should be noted that the traditional approach has visible benefits for the

traditional model, are as follows:

participation in multiple competitions over the entire season;  
(3) monitoring can be more efficient because of the substantial reduction in the 
number of athletic abilities to be evaluated within each mesocycle;  
(4) the diet and restorative program can be appropriately modified according 
to the predominant type of training and, finally,  
(5) a multi-stage annual plan creates more favorable conditions for peaking in 
time for the main competition of the season.

Example. The principle of unity of general and specialized preparation 
was postulated in the traditional theory in regard to high level performance.  
Training downplayed the importance of event-specific means during long periods 
of general preparation, where this specificity could be ignored.  Conversely, the 
importance of general exercises could be ignored during long competitive periods, 
when specific means are predominant. 
 
The principle of continuity was relevant when athletes lost motivation to 
train during long periods of monotonous training long before serious competition. 
The principle of wave-shape training was important to prevent overloading so 
prevalent during prolonged periods of hard workloads typical of traditional 
planning.  
  
 
The traditional design is still appropriate for low-level athletes.  It does not 
work well for high-performance athletes. Traditional theory also contains a number of 
contradictions which dramatically reduce preparation effectiveness.  (See table 1.4).  
 
For instance, preparatory period training for high level athletes in endurance 
sports, martial arts, dual and team sports and aesthetic sports, assumes the 
development of general aerobic abilities, muscle strength and strength endurance, 
improvement in general coordination and explosive ability, basic mental and technical 
preparation, mastery of the tactical repertory, and treatment of previous injuries. Each 
of these factors requires specific physiological, morphological and psychological 
adaptation.  However many of the workloads are not compatible and create 
conflicting responses.

content.content:
=== idx 32 ===
21
 
 
- 
Highly concentrated training workloads for many qualities cannot be managed 
at the same time.  Therefore, the training block is an alternative to the 
widespread practice of simultaneous complex development of many abilities; 
- 
Athletic performance in any sport usually demands the mastery of many 
abilities, which, in the case of training blocks, can only be developed 
consecutively, not concurrently; 
- 
Developing a process that includes morphological, organic and biochemical 
changes requires a sufficiently long time period of about 2-6 weeks, which 
corresponds to the duration of mesocycles.  Hence, training blocks are mostly 
mesocycle-blocks.   
 
One of the most successful coaches to achieve great results using this 
alternative training system was Anatoly Bondarchuk, who coached the gold-, silver-, 
and bronze-medal winners in the hammer throw at the 1988 and other Olympic 
Games.  He fulfilled the nearly unattainable dream of having the entire Olympic 
podium occupied by athletes of the same coach. Based on his own personal athletic 
experience (he was Olympic hammer throw champion in 1972) and careful 
investigation of throwers’ training programs (as part of his doctoral studies in 1988), 
Bondarchuk created the original periodization chart that completely reformed the 
traditional approaches to training (Bondarchuk, 1986 and 1988).  
 
Dr. Bondarchuk established three types of specialized mesocycle-blocks: 
developmental, where workload levels gradually increase to maximum; competitive, 
where the load level is stabilized and athletes focus on the competitive performance; 
and restorative, where athletes utilize active recovery and prepare for the next 
developmental program. The duration of the two first types of mesocycles is usually 
four weeks while the third can be shortened to two weeks. The sequencing of these 
blocks depends on the competition schedule and on the responses of individual 
athletes. The outstanding characteristic of this training program design is alternation 
and repetition of the exercise repertory in each mesocycle-block (every four weeks). 
The terms of traditional periodization like “preparatory, competitive and transitory 
periods” were used, but the author noted that in his concept their essence is very 
different.

content.content:
=== idx 75 ===
64
 
 
 
The compatible combinations need to be clarified: 
1) According to the BPC, the workout program should contain no more than three 
training modalities (usually one dominant, the second one – compatible with the 
main purpose, the third one – a modality of technique/tactic improvement or 
restoration); 
2) It is postulated that 65-70% of the entire training time for the development 
workout should be devoted to one or two selected training modalities.  This 
condition is important for attaining high workload concentration and to produce 
sufficient stimulus for a desirable training effect; 
3) The typical frequency of workouts in high-performance training (6-12 a week) 
dictates certain conditions pertaining to the session subsequent to the key-
workout.  In the basic approach to training design there is a significant reduction 
in workload after the key-workout. The alternative approach, in which two 
consecutive key-workouts are planned, provides very high load concentrations 
which can be excessive; 
4) Workouts for muscle hypertrophy impose very special demands when planning 
consecutive sessions within the restoration period.  The use of high workloads 
during this period adversely affects the anabolic phase of muscle restoration and 
eliminates the hypertrophy process. Thus, to attain the anabolic effect it is 
necessary to substantially reduce workloads for at least 20 hours and to utilize 
appropriate restoration means; 
5) Limiting the number of training modalities is particularly relevant in high-
performance sport.  For example, the daily program for juniors may be more 
diverse, multilateral and, therefore, more attractive.  
 
 
It is worth noting that reasonably combined exercises allow coaches to 
emphasize the acute effect of the dominant training modality and/or to exploit the 
effect of previous exercises in subsequent workloads. A number of these favorable 
psycho-physiological interactions is shown in Table 2.12.

1	---
2	type: library-entry

6	chapter: "1.2.2"
7	topic: workload concentration principle

11	created: 2026-09-26
12	---
13	
14	# Concentration of Training Workloads Is the Cornerstone Principle of Block Periodization
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin states the Block Periodization Concept (BPC) rests on one
17	foundational principle, concentration of training workloads, from which two others follow:
18	(1) a minimal number of targeted abilities per block, because highly concentrated loads
19	"only provide sufficient training stimuli to improve the targeted ability," and (2)
20	consecutive (not simultaneous) development of abilities, because "the number of decisive
21	abilities exceeds the number of abilities that can be developed simultaneously" (PDF p. 37,
22	printed p. 26, Figure 1.7). The rationale is laid out as a table of contradictions in the
23	traditional, simultaneous-development model for high-level athletes (Table 1.4, PDF p. 20,
24	printed p. 9): energy supply gets spread across too many targets so the main one does not
25	get the attention it needs, differing physiological-system restoration times leave athletes
26	under-recovered for all targets at once, workloads interact negatively (energy deficits,
27	technical complexity, neuromuscular fatigue), mental concentration cannot be split across
28	many targets, and the training stimulus needed for a high-level athlete's progress cannot be
29	reached when it is divided among many abilities. **Locator note:** Table 1.4's
30	Contradictions column literally reads "There is sufficient energy supply for concurrent
31	performance of diversified workloads" (PDF p. 20, printed p. 9); its Consequences column
32	implies the opposite, "Energy is directed to many targets while the main target doesn't get
33	the appropriate attention." This reads as an apparent wording inconsistency in the source;
34	the table's overall point, that concentration protects the main target's stimulus, still
35	stands.
36	
37	**Why it works** — Issurin's own explanation is that above a threshold of athletic level,

# Concentration of Training Workloads Is the Cornerstone Principle of Block Periodization

**What it is** — Issurin states the Block Periodization Concept (BPC) rests on one
foundational principle, concentration of training workloads, from which two others follow:
(1) a minimal number of targeted abilities per block, because highly concentrated loads
"only provide sufficient training stimuli to improve the targeted ability," and (2)
consecutive (not simultaneous) development of abilities, because "the number of decisive
abilities exceeds the number of abilities that can be developed simultaneously" (PDF p. 37,
printed p. 26, Figure 1.7). The rationale is laid out as a table of contradictions in the
traditional, simultaneous-development model for high-level athletes (Table 1.4, PDF p. 20,
printed p. 9): energy supply gets spread across too many targets so the main one does not
get the attention it needs, differing physiological-system restoration times leave athletes
under-recovered for all targets at once, workloads interact negatively (energy deficits,
technical complexity, neuromuscular fatigue), mental concentration cannot be split across
many targets, and the training stimulus needed for a high-level athlete's progress cannot be
reached when it is divided among many abilities. **Locator note:** Table 1.4's
Contradictions column literally reads "There is sufficient energy supply for concurrent
performance of diversified workloads" (PDF p. 20, printed p. 9); its Consequences column
implies the opposite, "Energy is directed to many targets while the main target doesn't get
the appropriate attention." This reads as an apparent wording inconsistency in the source;
the table's overall point, that concentration protects the main target's stimulus, still
stands.

**Why it works** — Issurin's own explanation is that above a threshold of athletic level,
a quality only responds to a training stimulus concentrated enough to exceed that
threshold; splitting the same total training time across many qualities keeps each one's
stimulus below that threshold. He does not give a quantitative mechanism for where that
threshold sits or how "concentrated enough" is defined for a given ability or athlete; the
principle is argued from coaches' and scientists' collective experience (Table 1.4) rather
than derived from a stated dose-response model.

**When to apply** — Designing training blocks for advanced, high-level athletes juggling
more qualities than can be trained well at once (the explicit target population, per
Issurin). **Eric's baseline:** the course teaches this rule from Issurin directly
(week1-lecture.md marker pp.64, 67, which name "Issurin (Block Training Text)" as a source
for block periodization and file "you can't ride 2 horses w/one saddle" under the same
section), not as an independent convergence: "you can't ride two horses with one saddle",
incompatible qualities are not both trained at full intensity in the same block
(`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.28-29). It also converges with
[[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]], which independently
describes concentrated, saturated loading on one quality with a delayed 4-12 week rebound.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — Issurin's own text (PDF p. 44, printed p. 33) states the
traditional, complex (simultaneous multi-ability) model "has visible benefits for the
preparation of low- and mid-level athletes": it is "more diversified, attractive and
lively," and medium-level concentration is "sufficient stimulation" at that level: the
concentration principle is explicitly scoped to high-performance athletes, not a universal
programming rule. **Contested:** Issurin's blanket claim elsewhere in the same chapter that
the traditional model "does not work well for high-performance athletes" (PDF p. 19,
printed p. 8) is disputed by Issurin's own later peer-reviewed review (Issurin, 2016,
*Sports Medicine*, "Benefits and Limitations of Block Periodized Training Approaches to
Athletes' Preparation," Zotero item `PT9QTQ2I`, full text cached in this library at
`research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a.md`):
that review judges concentrated-unidirectional block programs' evidence insufficient for
broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation, and
frames the concentrated-unidirectional model as restricted when peak performance requires
many interacting abilities (its p.6, p.11), a real narrowing of this 2008 book's confident
"does not work well for high-performance athletes" framing, for exactly the population this
principle targets. **Inference:** Bompa & Haff's 5th edition, already in this library, may
also bear on this claim, but only Bompa Ch1-2 has been ingested so far
(`periodization--bompa/_book.md`: Ch6 Annual Plan and Ch8 Training Cycles are pending); the
one relevant ingested entry, `principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching`, *converges*
with Issurin rather than disputing him, so it cannot be used to ground this contest. Check
whether Bompa & Haff Ch6-8 defend period-based annual planning for high-level athletes once
those chapters are ingested. Issurin's critique in this chapter also names Bompa's *1984*
edition specifically (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2) as one of the texts that propagated the
traditional model he is arguing against; that is a different, narrower target than the 5th
edition.

**Example** — **Inference:** a collegiate football strength staff trying to develop max strength,
aerobic capacity, alactic power, and technical skill acquisition all at full intensity in
the same 4-week block, per Table 1.4's logic, risks under-stimulating all four rather than
meaningfully improving any one; concentrating the block on 1-2 of them (with the rest held
at a retention dose) is the alternative Issurin argues for.

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]], the three-block
structure this principle produces. [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]]
and [[periodization--bompa/framework--step-loading-paradigm]], converging concentrated-load
ideas already in this library. [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (staging):
check for overlap on why generalized simultaneous training under-delivers for advanced
athletes.

routines during prolonged block ‘A’. Perhaps such plan-

The further explanation of CU training system presup-
poses a load sequencing that progressed from power/
strength development (2–3 months) to more specialized
sport-speciﬁc improvement (2 months) and event-speciﬁc

practice (3–5 weeks). The author called this three-block
sequence (i.e., blocks ‘A’, ‘B’, and ‘C’) the ‘‘big adaptation
cycle’’, the duration of which was 22–26 weeks [10, 12].
The CU training system was proposed as an innovative
approach for high-performance athletes, when load regu-

play but, in particular, with proper structuring of the
training program content. In fact the ‘three block unity’
offers a reasonable and realistic framework for annual
planning. However, their time span allows the inclusion of
two ‘big adaptation cycles’ per year, which correspond-
ingly means implementation of a two-peak annual design.
Viewed in this light, this innovative version has no
advantage over traditional planning, because it does not
allow the multi-peak annual design demanded for effective
preparation of high-performance athletes.
2.2 Evidence of Studies Evaluating the CU Training
Model
Over recent decades, a number of studies have been con-
ducted around the world aimed at evaluating the effect of
CU training in different sports (Table 2).
The ﬁrst study listed in Table 2 presented a comparison
of traditional and BP training models for shootboxers [13].
The CU program consisted of sequenced blocks intended to
develop endurance, maximal strength, explosive strength,
technique and rapidity, and, ﬁnally, speciﬁc endurance.
Statistical treatment revealed the superiority of the BP
group only in speciﬁc endurance, the development of
which was completed towards the last part of the program.
The authors concluded that the BP training model was only
partially applicable to the needs of the athletes under study.
The next three studies were conducted with elite bas-
ketball, handball, and soccer players [14–16] and included
sequenced training blocks of highly CU workloads. In all
these cases, prolonged BP programs resulted in signiﬁcant
enhancement of various ﬁtness estimates; however, the
researchers did not report the effects of the programs on
team practice and competitive activities. Unfortunately, the
investigators appeared to not consider the possible impact

mastery of elite athletes.
The experiment with elite swimmers revealed remark-
able gains in speciﬁc strength and anaerobic capacity,
whereas swimming performance was enhanced in only two
of the three subjects—a relatively small sample to begin
with [17].

quate research methods and appropriate statistical treat-

sufﬁcient evidence for further implementation of the CU
BP approach in preparing high-performance athletes in

# Concentration of Training Workloads Is the Cornerstone Principle of Block Periodization

**What it is** — Issurin states the Block Periodization Concept (BPC) rests on one
foundational principle, concentration of training workloads, from which two others follow:
(1) a minimal number of targeted abilities per block, because highly concentrated loads
"only provide sufficient training stimuli to improve the targeted ability," and (2)
consecutive (not simultaneous) development of abilities, because "the number of decisive
abilities exceeds the number of abilities that can be developed simultaneously" (PDF p. 37,
printed p. 26, Figure 1.7). The rationale is laid out as a table of contradictions in the
traditional, simultaneous-development model for high-level athletes (Table 1.4, PDF p. 20,
printed p. 9): energy supply gets spread across too many targets so the main one does not
get the attention it needs, differing physiological-system restoration times leave athletes
under-recovered for all targets at once, workloads interact negatively (energy deficits,
technical complexity, neuromuscular fatigue), mental concentration cannot be split across
many targets, and the training stimulus needed for a high-level athlete's progress cannot be
reached when it is divided among many abilities. **Locator note:** Table 1.4's
Contradictions column literally reads "There is sufficient energy supply for concurrent
performance of diversified workloads" (PDF p. 20, printed p. 9); its Consequences column
implies the opposite, "Energy is directed to many targets while the main target doesn't get
the appropriate attention." This reads as an apparent wording inconsistency in the source;
the table's overall point, that concentration protects the main target's stimulus, still
stands.

**Why it works** — Issurin's own explanation is that above a threshold of athletic level,
a quality only responds to a training stimulus concentrated enough to exceed that
threshold; splitting the same total training time across many qualities keeps each one's
stimulus below that threshold. He does not give a quantitative mechanism for where that
threshold sits or how "concentrated enough" is defined for a given ability or athlete; the
principle is argued from coaches' and scientists' collective experience (Table 1.4) rather
than derived from a stated dose-response model.

**When to apply** — Designing training blocks for advanced, high-level athletes juggling
more qualities than can be trained well at once (the explicit target population, per
Issurin). **Eric's baseline:** the course teaches this rule from Issurin directly
(week1-lecture.md marker pp.64, 67, which name "Issurin (Block Training Text)" as a source
for block periodization and file "you can't ride 2 horses w/one saddle" under the same
section), not as an independent convergence: "you can't ride two horses with one saddle",
incompatible qualities are not both trained at full intensity in the same block
(`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.28-29). It also converges with
[[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]], which independently
describes concentrated, saturated loading on one quality with a delayed 4-12 week rebound.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — Issurin's own text (PDF p. 44, printed p. 33) states the
traditional, complex (simultaneous multi-ability) model "has visible benefits for the
preparation of low- and mid-level athletes": it is "more diversified, attractive and
lively," and medium-level concentration is "sufficient stimulation" at that level: the
concentration principle is explicitly scoped to high-performance athletes, not a universal
programming rule. **Contested:** Issurin's blanket claim elsewhere in the same chapter that
the traditional model "does not work well for high-performance athletes" (PDF p. 19,
printed p. 8) is disputed by Issurin's own later peer-reviewed review (Issurin, 2016,
*Sports Medicine*, "Benefits and Limitations of Block Periodized Training Approaches to
Athletes' Preparation," Zotero item `PT9QTQ2I`, full text cached in this library at
`research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a.md`):
that review judges concentrated-unidirectional block programs' evidence insufficient for
broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation, and
frames the concentrated-unidirectional model as restricted when peak performance requires
many interacting abilities (its p.6, p.11), a real narrowing of this 2008 book's confident
"does not work well for high-performance athletes" framing, for exactly the population this
principle targets. **Inference:** Bompa & Haff's 5th edition, already in this library, may
also bear on this claim, but only Bompa Ch1-2 has been ingested so far
(`periodization--bompa/_book.md`: Ch6 Annual Plan and Ch8 Training Cycles are pending); the
one relevant ingested entry, `principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching`, *converges*
with Issurin rather than disputing him, so it cannot be used to ground this contest. Check
whether Bompa & Haff Ch6-8 defend period-based annual planning for high-level athletes once
those chapters are ingested. Issurin's critique in this chapter also names Bompa's *1984*
edition specifically (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2) as one of the texts that propagated the
traditional model he is arguing against; that is a different, narrower target than the 5th
edition.

aerobic capacity, alactic power, and technical skill acquisition all at full intensity in

meaningfully improving any one; concentrating the block on 1-2 of them (with the rest held
at a retention dose) is the alternative Issurin argues for.

and [[periodization--bompa/framework--step-loading-paradigm]], converging concentrated-load

# Concentration of Training Workloads Is the Cornerstone Principle of Block Periodization

20	(accumulation), one resembling a competition period (transmutation), and a tapering block

25	months," though Issurin notes stages can run shorter near season's end or longer earlier in
26	the season, in which case "special measures should be used to prolong residual training
27	effects" (unspecified in this chapter; developed in Chapter 3, now ingested, see `_book.md`).
28	The number of training stages in a season "usually varies from four to seven," depending on
29	the sport's competition calendar (PDF p. 40, printed p. 29, Figure 1.9). Issurin lists four
30	benefits of this design over the traditional model at this point in the text (PDF p. 40,
31	printed p. 29): the model allows a reduction in total mileage and time spent training
32	without substantially changing the total number of workouts; monitoring of trainedness is
33	more purposeful and effective, because the reduced number of targeted abilities allows more
34	appropriate tests and an easier dose-effect analysis; psychological traits improve because
35	athletes can focus on fewer abilities, supporting mental concentration and motivation; and
36	nutritional aspects can be more carefully targeted (a high-protein diet to enhance strength
37	training's anabolic effect, and carbohydrates "particularly important in mesocycles for
38	specialized and strength-endurance" work). Table 1.8 (PDF p. 42, printed p. 31) is a

43	competition of the season," with intermediate peaks plannable mid-season or even early
44	season, not only at a single season-end date.

**What it is** — Issurin's annual cycle is built from a sequence of **training stages**,
each one containing all three mesocycle-blocks (accumulation, transmutation, realization) in
order, ending in a competition (PDF p. 38, printed p. 27). Each training stage "gives the
appearance of an annual cycle in miniature", a block resembling a preparatory period

ending in competitive performance (realization) (PDF p. 39, printed p. 28). The duration of
a training stage is set by how long the constituent residual training effects can be
superimposed (Figure 1.8; see
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]) and "should be about two
months," though Issurin notes stages can run shorter near season's end or longer earlier in
the season, in which case "special measures should be used to prolong residual training
effects" (unspecified in this chapter; developed in Chapter 3, now ingested, see `_book.md`).
The number of training stages in a season "usually varies from four to seven," depending on
the sport's competition calendar (PDF p. 40, printed p. 29, Figure 1.9). Issurin lists four
benefits of this design over the traditional model at this point in the text (PDF p. 40,
printed p. 29): the model allows a reduction in total mileage and time spent training
without substantially changing the total number of workouts; monitoring of trainedness is
more purposeful and effective, because the reduced number of targeted abilities allows more
appropriate tests and an easier dose-effect analysis; psychological traits improve because
athletes can focus on fewer abilities, supporting mental concentration and motivation; and
nutritional aspects can be more carefully targeted (a high-protein diet to enhance strength
training's anabolic effect, and carbohydrates "particularly important in mesocycles for
specialized and strength-endurance" work). Table 1.8 (PDF p. 42, printed p. 31) is a
separate table contrasting the traditional and Block Periodization models' main differences,
not itself a benefits list. A second, five-item benefit summary appears later in the chapter
(PDF p. 44, printed p. 33), largely repeating the first four points and adding a fifth: "a
multi-stage annual plan creates more favorable conditions for peaking in time for the main
competition of the season," with intermediate peaks plannable mid-season or even early
season, not only at a single season-end date.

**Why it works** — Because each training stage runs its own compressed
accumulation-transmutation-realization cycle and ends in a real competitive test, the athlete
is brought to a peak (or near-peak) at the end of every stage rather than once per year;
stacking four to seven such stages across a season is what produces the multi-peak pattern.
Issurin's stated physiological contrast (Table 1.8) is that the traditional model relies on
adaptation to concurrent stimuli across a long period, while this model relies on
superimposing sequential residual effects from short, concentrated blocks; the same
mechanism underlies [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]].

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is the entry most directly responsive to the strength-and-conditioning
miss-log gap ("peaking phase structure for collegiate football," logged 2026-09-03): for a
football program needing camp-readiness, then in-season week-to-week competitive readiness,
this framework suggests treating each significant test point (fall camp scrimmage, each
game week, or a defined in-season block) as a candidate training-stage boundary rather than
relying on a single annual peak, with the caveat below about untested claims. **Eric's
baseline** does not currently describe an explicit training-stage or multi-peak model for
football; the closest baseline material is the general macro/meso/microcycle planning
language and the in-season rule "maintain intensity, reduce volume" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Periodization and programming" and "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.17-18, 20-21). This Issurin framework offers a
more explicit structural answer to "how do you actually sequence a season with more than one
peak" than anything currently captured in the baseline.

figures are stated without a derivation the reader can check: Issurin gives no worked
example of how stage count or duration is calculated for a specific sport's calendar in
this chapter. **Inference:** football's in-season structure (weekly games, not discrete
multi-week competition-free blocks) does not map cleanly onto a ~2-month training stage.
Issurin's model is built from and mainly evidenced by individual/dual sports with discrete
competitions (track and field, canoe-kayak, windsurfing); Chapter 3's microcycle-level
material (now ingested; see `_book.md`) is a necessary next read before this framework can
be translated into a week-by-week in-season football plan. **Contested:** Issurin's "does
not work well for high-performance athletes" framing of the traditional alternative (PDF p.
19, printed p. 8, the same claim flagged in
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]) is disputed by Issurin's own later
peer-reviewed review (Issurin, 2016, *Sports Medicine*, "Benefits and Limitations of Block
Periodized Training Approaches to Athletes' Preparation," Zotero item `PT9QTQ2I`, full text
cached in this library at
`research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a.md`).
That review reports that concentrated-unidirectional programs in team and combat sports
improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team
practice or competitive performance (its p.6): a direct qualification of the confident
five-benefit list above, for exactly the team-sport context football sits in. **Inference:**

earlier in the season, in which case "special measures should be used to prolong residual
training effects" (developed in Chapter 3, now ingested; see
[[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]] and `_book.md`).
The number of training stages in a season "usually varies from four to seven," depending on
the sport's competition calendar (PDF p. 40, printed p. 29, Figure 1.9). Issurin lists four
benefits of this design over the traditional model at this point in the text (PDF p. 40,
printed p. 29): the model allows a reduction in total mileage and time spent training
without substantially changing the total number of workouts; monitoring of trainedness is
more purposeful and effective, because the reduced number of targeted abilities allows more
appropriate tests and an easier dose-effect analysis; psychological traits improve because
athletes can focus on fewer abilities, supporting mental concentration and motivation; and
nutritional aspects can be more carefully targeted (a high-protein diet to enhance strength
training's anabolic effect, and carbohydrates "particularly important in mesocycles for
specialized and strength-endurance" work). Table 1.8 (PDF p. 42, printed p. 31) is a
separate table contrasting the traditional and Block Periodization models' main differences,
not itself a benefits list. Separately, and also on that page (PDF p. 42, printed p. 31),
Issurin states the intermediate peaks "can be planned for mid-season and even for the early
part of the season," not only at a single season-end date. A second, five-item list appears
later in the chapter (PDF p. 44, printed p. 33) and differs from the first rather than
repeating it: it adds that total training volume "can be greatly reduced, minimizing the
incidence of overtraining," that the multi-peak design "facilitates successful participation
in multiple competitions over the entire season," and, as a fifth item, "a multi-stage annual
plan creates more favorable conditions for peaking in time for the main competition of the
season"; it keeps the monitoring and diet/restoration points from the first list but omits
the psychological benefit.

**Why it works** — Because each training stage runs its own compressed
accumulation-transmutation-realization cycle and ends in a real competitive test, the athlete
is brought to a peak (or near-peak) at the end of every stage rather than once per year;
stacking four to seven such stages across a season is what produces the multi-peak pattern.
Issurin's stated physiological contrast (Table 1.8) is that the traditional model relies on
adaptation to concurrent stimuli across a long period, while this model relies on
superimposing sequential residual effects from short, concentrated blocks; the same
mechanism underlies [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]].

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is the entry most directly responsive to the strength-and-conditioning
miss-log gap ("peaking phase structure for collegiate football," logged 2026-09-03): for a
football program needing camp-readiness, then in-season week-to-week competitive readiness,
this framework suggests treating each significant test point (fall camp scrimmage, each
game week, or a defined in-season block) as a candidate training-stage boundary rather than
relying on a single annual peak, with the caveat below about untested claims. **Eric's
baseline** does not currently describe an explicit training-stage or multi-peak model for
football; the closest baseline material is the general macro/meso/microcycle planning
language and the in-season rule "maintain intensity, reduce volume" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Periodization and programming" and "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.17-18, 20-21). This Issurin framework offers a
more explicit structural answer to "how do you actually sequence a season with more than one
peak" than anything currently captured in the baseline.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — The "four to seven stages" and "about two months"
figures are stated without a derivation the reader can check: Issurin gives no worked
example of how stage count or duration is calculated for a specific sport's calendar in
this chapter. **Inference:** football's in-season structure (weekly games, not discrete
multi-week competition-free blocks) does not map cleanly onto a ~2-month training stage.
Issurin's model is built from and mainly evidenced by individual/dual sports with discrete
competitions (track and field, canoe-kayak, windsurfing); Chapter 3's microcycle-level
material (now ingested; see `_book.md`) is a necessary next read before this framework can
be translated into a week-by-week in-season football plan. **Contested:** Issurin's "does
not work well for high-performance athletes" framing of the traditional alternative (PDF p.
19, printed p. 8, the same claim flagged in
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]) is disputed by Issurin's own later
peer-reviewed review (Issurin, 2016, *Sports Medicine*, "Benefits and Limitations of Block
Periodized Training Approaches to Athletes' Preparation," Zotero item `PT9QTQ2I`, full text
cached in this library at
`research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a.md`).
That review reports that concentrated-unidirectional programs in team and combat sports
improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team
practice or competitive performance (its p.6): a direct qualification of the confident
five-benefit list above, for exactly the team-sport context football sits in. **Inference:**
Bompa & Haff's 5th edition, already in this library, may also bear on the "does not work
well" claim, but only Bompa Ch1-2 has been ingested so far (`periodization--bompa/_book.md`:
Ch6 Annual Plan and Ch8 Training Cycles are pending), so it cannot ground this contest yet;
check once those chapters are ingested.

**Example** — **Inference:** a five-stage football off-season/camp plan: Stage 1 (general
accumulation, ~8 weeks, winter conditioning); Stage 2 (strength/power transmutation into
spring ball, ending in the spring game as a "competition"); Stage 3 (summer accumulation);
Stage 4 (fall-camp transmutation, ending in the first scrimmage or game week as
realization); Stage 5+ (in-season stages keyed to bye weeks or rivalry-week peaks, pending
Chapter 3's in-season microcycle guidance).

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[claim--multi-peak-annual-preparation-elite-track-and-field]] (the empirical motivation for
needing a multi-peak model), [[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]].

# Accumulation, Transmutation (Transformation), and Realization: the Three Mesocycle-Blocks

**What it is** — Issurin's core structural unit is the mesocycle-block, one of three types
(Table 1.7, PDF p. 38, printed p. 27): **Accumulation** targets basic abilities (aerobic
endurance, muscular strength, basic coordination) with high volume/reduced intensity and
"reasonable restoration"; **Transmutation** targets sport-specific abilities (special
endurance, strength endurance, proper technique) with reduced volume/increased intensity,
and explicitly does *not* provide full restoration: fatigue accumulates; **Realization**
targets integrative, competition-ready preparedness (model performances, maximum speed,
event-specific tactics) at low-medium volume/high intensity, with full restoration required
going in. Each type has its own monitoring focus: basic-ability tests for accumulation,
sport-specific-ability tests for transmutation, and maximum speed/strategy checks for
realization. Original prescribed durations: about four weeks each for accumulation and
transformation, two weeks for realization (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22); more generally,
mesocycle-blocks run about 2-6 weeks, the time needed for morphological, organic, and
biochemical adaptation (PDF p. 32, printed p. 21). **Locator note:** the 1985 origin paper
(Issurin & Kaverin) and this book's 1.2.1 narrative (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22) use the term
**transformation**; from section 1.2.2 onward, starting at PDF p. 38, printed p. 27 (not
p.26 as the offset alone would suggest), and in the book's own tables, the term used is
**transmutation**. Both names refer to the same middle block; record both because a search
for either term should resolve to this entry.

**Why it works** — The sequencing is designed to exploit the fact that different motor
abilities have different **residual training effect** durations (see
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]): basic abilities (aerobic
endurance, max strength) decay slowest, so they can be built early and coast on their own
residual while transmutation and realization narrow the focus toward faster-decaying,
more specific and speed-dependent qualities close to competition. Issurin frames this as
superimposition of residual effects (Figure 1.8, PDF p. 39, printed p. 28) rather than
concurrent development of everything at once.

**When to apply** — Structuring a training stage (the accumulation-transmutation-realization
sequence, ending in competition) for advanced athletes who need multiple qualities peaked
together; see [[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]] for how these three
blocks compose into a full annual plan. **Eric's baseline:** the course teaches
accumulation/transmutation/realization directly from Issurin (week1-lecture.md marker p.65,
in the same slide block that names "Issurin (Block Training Text)" as a source, marker
p.64). The department's own preparatory-period design, hypertrophy/work-capacity, then basic
strength, then strength-to-power (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming,"
citing week1-lecture.md pp.43-48), is a separate general-to-specific progression, not a
restatement of A-T-R; it is not explicitly framed with Issurin's residual-effect
superimposition logic or his restoration-status distinctions between blocks.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — This is a three-way classification built for advanced
athletes who can tolerate the fatigue-accumulating transmutation block (see
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] for the low-/mid-level-athlete
carve-out). It presumes a training stage that ends in a real competition or test date to
absorb the realization block's tapering logic; without a fixed target date, there is no
clear trigger for when accumulation should end and transmutation begin. **Inference (beyond
this review's scope, flagged during this fix pass since it repeats the same Bompa problem
found in [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]):** the vault's Bompa & Haff
material (`periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching`) describes a
comparable saturated-load-then-restitution structure with a 4-12 week delayed rebound, a
longer and less rigidly three-staged model than Issurin's roughly two-month training stage
(below); the two should be read as convergent, not identical, prescriptions, and a program
note should say which model's timing a given plan follows.

**Example** — **Inference:** a training stage built for a mid-season peak using the book's
own prescribed durations (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22): about 4 weeks of accumulation (aerobic
base, general strength), about 4 weeks of transmutation (sport-specific conditioning,
strength-endurance, technique under fatigue), then 2 weeks of realization (tapered volume,
high-intensity model-speed work, full restoration) ending at the target competition or test
date.

**Related** — [[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],
[[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]],
[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]] (a different three-block taxonomy
from the same era, worth distinguishing from this one),
[[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]],
[[periodization--bompa/framework--step-loading-paradigm]].

1	---
2	type: library-entry
3	kind: claim
4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
5	book: block-periodization--issurin
6	chapter: "1.2.1"
7	topic: residual training effect durations
8	category: [periodization, detraining, adaptation, programming]
9	confidence: contested
10	ingest-tier: full-text
11	created: 2026-09-26
12	---
13	
14	# Residual Training Effects Last Different Numbers of Days for Different Motor Abilities
15	
16	**What it is** — The residual training effect is defined as "the retention of changes
17	induced by systematic workloads beyond a certain time period after the cessation of
18	training," a term Issurin attributes to Brian and James Counsilman (1991) (PDF p. 33,
19	printed p. 22). Issurin & Lustig (2004) is cited as the source of Table 1.6 (PDF p. 35,
20	printed p. 24), giving residual duration ± SD in days after cessation of training for each
21	motor ability: **aerobic endurance 30 ± 5 days**, **maximum strength 30 ± 5 days**,
22	**anaerobic glycolytic endurance 18 ± 4 days**, **strength endurance 15 ± 5 days**,
23	**maximum speed (alactic) 5 ± 3 days**. Table 1.6's own physiological-background column
24	lists aerobic endurance's residual as resting on increased aerobic enzymes, mitochondria,
25	muscle capillaries, hemoglobin capacity, glycogen storage, and fat-metabolism rate, and
26	maximum strength's on improved neural mechanism and muscle hypertrophy from fiber
27	enlargement, with no percentages attached in the table itself. Later in the text (PDF p. 35,
28	printed p. 24), Issurin gives a specific figure for one of those table items: aerobic
29	enzymes increase by 40-90% with training (Volkov, 1986; Fox et al., 1993; Wilmore & Costill,
30	1993). He contrasts this with much smaller local adaptations from sprint training:
31	phosphocreatine storage (+2-5%), peak lactate accumulation (+10-20%), and anaerobic enzymes
32	(+2-20%), given without a citation on that page. On the following page (PDF p. 36, printed
33	p. 25), Thorstensson (1988) is cited specifically for "relatively small increases" in
34	quickly available energy sources, ATP and phosphocreatine, and enzymes such as creatine
35	kinase, from highly concentrated sprint training.
36	
37	**Why it works** — Issurin states the mechanism directly (PDF pp. 35-36, printed pp. 24-25):
38	aerobic ability, supported by pronounced morphological and biochemical changes, is retained
39	"for a number of weeks at near-peak level," while anaerobic abilities, particularly maximum
40	sprint speed, "retain near-peak levels for much shorter periods" because peak speed's gains
41	are smaller and rest on "very delicate and highly precise neuro-muscular interactions, which
42	are relatively unstable and cannot be maintained at the highest level without specially
43	organized training." Maximum strength's comparably long residual is attributed to pronounced
44	morphological, biochemical, and neural changes: enlargement of muscle-fiber cross-sectional
45	area, hyperplasia, recruitment of previously inactive motor units, synchronization of their
46	activity, and increased motor-neuron discharge frequency (Zatsiorsky, 1995). Strength
47	endurance's residual is stated to depend on event duration and the degree of
48	anaerobic-resource mobilization; longer-duration strength endurance has a relatively longer
49	residual thanks to aerobic adaptation.
50	
51	**When to apply** — Sequencing which ability to develop first in a training stage (see
52	[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]): an ability with a long
53	residual (aerobic endurance, max strength) can be built early in accumulation and largely
54	coast through transmutation/realization without a maintenance dose, while an ability with a
55	short residual (max speed) needs re-exposure close to competition or its gain will be lost
56	before it is used. **Eric's baseline directly echoes half of this table:** "Training
57	residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need
58	re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue
59	readiness for max-velocity work degrades" (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and
60	programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` p.27). This 30/30/5-day
61	pattern matches Issurin's 30±5 / 30±5 / 5±3 figures because it is this table:
62	week1-lecture.md (marker p.66) reproduces Table 1.6 directly, under a slide block that names
63	"Issurin (Block Training Text)" as a source (marker p.64), and gives strength endurance as
64	~12 days against Issurin's 15±5, the one value where the course departs from the book.
65	
66	**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — Treat the numbers as a synthesized rule of thumb
67	(±5, ±4, ±5, ±3 day spreads are themselves wide relative to the means), not a precise
68	per-athlete clock; Issurin does not report the sample or method behind Issurin & Lustig
69	(2004) in this text, so the table's evidentiary base cannot be checked further from this
70	source alone. Issurin's own surrounding text also notes limits on how far residual-effect
71	thinking travels: maximum oxygen uptake in highly trained endurance athletes falls when
72	weekly training volume drops below a certain level (Steinacker, 1993; Steinacker et al.,
73	1998), and large volumes of highly intense exercise do not prevent detraining and loss of
74	aerobic endurance during a taper (Mujika, 1999) (PDF p. 34, printed p. 23).
75	
76	**Contested, flag this directly to Eric:** a *different* part of the same baseline corpus
77	states the opposite ordering for detraining rate: "the traits easiest to build (aerobic) are
78	lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest"
79	(`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md` p.47).
80	This conflicts with Table 1.6 (aerobic residual is the *longest*, tied with strength, at
81	30±5 days, while alactic speed is the *shortest* at 5±3 days). The class-1 transcript is
82	not a third, independent data point against class-4-2026.md: it also states that aerobic
83	capacity is gained and lost very quickly (marker pp.25, 28), gives its 30-day retention
84	windows as conditional on "a small retention load" continuing during that window (marker
85	p.28), a different construct from Issurin's residual *after cessation* of training, and
