# Residual Training Effects Last Different Numbers of Days for Different Motor Abilities

**What it is** — The residual training effect is defined as "the retention of changes
induced by systematic workloads beyond a certain time period after the cessation of
training," a term Issurin attributes to Brian and James Counsilman (1991) (PDF p. 33,
printed p. 22). Issurin & Lustig (2004) is cited as the source of Table 1.6 (PDF p. 35,
printed p. 24), giving residual duration ± SD in days after cessation of training for each
motor ability: **aerobic endurance 30 ± 5 days**, **maximum strength 30 ± 5 days**,
**anaerobic glycolytic endurance 18 ± 4 days**, **strength endurance 15 ± 5 days**,
**maximum speed (alactic) 5 ± 3 days**. Table 1.6's own physiological-background column
lists aerobic endurance's residual as resting on increased aerobic enzymes, mitochondria,
muscle capillaries, hemoglobin capacity, glycogen storage, and fat-metabolism rate, and
maximum strength's on improved neural mechanism and muscle hypertrophy from fiber
enlargement, with no percentages attached in the table itself. Later in the text (PDF p. 35,
printed p. 24), Issurin gives a specific figure for one of those table items: aerobic
enzymes increase by 40-90% with training (Volkov, 1986; Fox et al., 1993; Wilmore & Costill,
1993). He contrasts this with much smaller local adaptations from sprint training:
phosphocreatine storage (+2-5%), peak lactate accumulation (+10-20%), and anaerobic enzymes
(+2-20%), given without a citation on that page. On the following page (PDF p. 36, printed
p. 25), Thorstensson (1988) is cited specifically for "relatively small increases" in
quickly available energy sources, ATP and phosphocreatine, and enzymes such as creatine
kinase, from highly concentrated sprint training.

**Why it works** — Issurin states the mechanism directly (PDF pp. 35-36, printed pp. 24-25):
aerobic ability, supported by pronounced morphological and biochemical changes, is retained
"for a number of weeks at near-peak level," while anaerobic abilities, particularly maximum
sprint speed, "retain near-peak levels for much shorter periods" because peak speed's gains
are smaller and rest on "very delicate and highly precise neuro-muscular interactions, which
are relatively unstable and cannot be maintained at the highest level without specially
organized training." Maximum strength's comparably long residual is attributed to pronounced
morphological, biochemical, and neural changes: enlargement of muscle-fiber cross-sectional
area, hyperplasia, recruitment of previously inactive motor units, synchronization of their
activity, and increased motor-neuron discharge frequency (Zatsiorsky, 1995). Strength
endurance's residual is stated to depend on event duration and the degree of
anaerobic-resource mobilization; longer-duration strength endurance has a relatively longer
residual thanks to aerobic adaptation.

**When to apply** — Sequencing which ability to develop first in a training stage (see
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]): an ability with a long
residual (aerobic endurance, max strength) can be built early in accumulation and largely
coast through transmutation/realization without a maintenance dose, while an ability with a
short residual (max speed) needs re-exposure close to competition or its gain will be lost
before it is used. **Eric's baseline directly echoes half of this table:** "Training
residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need
re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue
readiness for max-velocity work degrades" (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and
programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` p.27). This 30/30/5-day
pattern matches Issurin's 30±5 / 30±5 / 5±3 figures because it is this table:
week1-lecture.md (marker p.66) reproduces Table 1.6 directly, under a slide block that names
"Issurin (Block Training Text)" as a source (marker p.64), and gives strength endurance as
~12 days against Issurin's 15±5, the one value where the course departs from the book.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — Treat the numbers as a synthesized rule of thumb
(±5, ±4, ±5, ±3 day spreads are themselves wide relative to the means), not a precise
per-athlete clock; Issurin does not report the sample or method behind Issurin & Lustig
(2004) in this text, so the table's evidentiary base cannot be checked further from this
source alone. Issurin's own surrounding text also notes limits on how far residual-effect
thinking travels: maximum oxygen uptake in highly trained endurance athletes falls when
weekly training volume drops below a certain level (Steinacker, 1993; Steinacker et al.,
1998), and large volumes of highly intense exercise do not prevent detraining and loss of
aerobic endurance during a taper (Mujika, 1999) (PDF p. 34, printed p. 23).

**Contested, flag this directly to Eric:** a *different* part of the same baseline corpus
states the opposite ordering for detraining rate: "the traits easiest to build (aerobic) are
lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md` p.47).
This conflicts with Table 1.6 (aerobic residual is the *longest*, tied with strength, at
30±5 days, while alactic speed is the *shortest* at 5±3 days). The class-1 transcript is
not a third, independent data point against class-4-2026.md: it also states that aerobic
capacity is gained and lost very quickly (marker pp.25, 28), gives its 30-day retention
windows as conditional on "a small retention load" continuing during that window (marker
p.28), a different construct from Issurin's residual *after cessation* of training, and
ties its 5-day speed figure to connective-tissue and nervous-system readiness ("otherwise
the nervous system doesn't change a whole lot," marker p.28) rather than to speed itself
decaying in 5 days. The course's own numbers come directly from this table (week1-lecture.md
marker pp.64, 66, strength endurance given there as ~12 days against Issurin's 15±5). Resolve
with Eric: this may be residual effect after cessation (Issurin, Table 1.6) versus rate of
loss without any retention dose (class-4-2026.md), two different constructs the corpus does
not itself reconcile. Do not harmonize these; record all three with their locators and keep
`contested`, with this as the stated reason.

**Inference:** this table also converges with, but is not identical to, the vault's
Verkhoshansky-staging entry on heterochronic adaptation
([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]],
staging), which describes a *different* mechanism (order of biochemical sub-processes
gained/lost) rather than absolute day-counts per motor ability; both describe
heterochronicity in de-training, but at different levels of description; do not treat them
as restating the same specific claim.

**Example** — **Inference:** in a training stage that opens with 4 weeks of accumulation
(building aerobic base and max strength) followed by 3 weeks of transmutation and 2 weeks of
realization, competition falls 35 days after accumulation ends: at the outer edge of the
aerobic and strength residuals' 30 ± 5-day window, not safely inside it. A coach relying on
this table would want a maintenance dose of both qualities somewhere in transmutation, not
an assumption that accumulation-phase gains are still fully in hand. Maximum speed work
needs re-introduction within about 5 days of the target competition, or its residual will
have decayed well below peak by competition day.

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]] (a ratio-based rule for
fatigue-vs-fitness decay, distinct from this table's absolute per-ability day counts:
cross-reference, do not conflate),
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] (staging),
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]] (staging).

14	# Case Study: Bondarchuk's Developmental/Competitive/Restorative Blocks and the 1988 Hammer Throw Podium
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin credits Anatoly Bondarchuk, hammer-throw coach, with one of the
17	precursor systems to Block Periodization (PDF p. 32, printed p. 21). Based on his own
18	athletic career (1972 Olympic hammer-throw champion) and doctoral research on throwers'
19	training programs (1988), Bondarchuk built a periodization chart using three types of
20	specialized mesocycle-blocks: **developmental** (workload gradually increases to maximum),
21	**competitive** (load stabilizes, athletes focus on competitive performance), and
22	**restorative** (active recovery, preparing for the next developmental block). Stated
23	durations: developmental and competitive blocks are "usually four weeks," restorative "can
24	be shortened to two weeks." Sequencing depends on the competition schedule and individual
25	athlete response. The book also gives what it calls Bondarchuk's design's outstanding
26	characteristic: alternation and repetition of the exercise repertory in each mesocycle-block
27	(every four weeks); the traditional period names, preparatory, competitive, and transitory,
28	were kept, but Issurin notes "their essence is very different" in Bondarchuk's concept (PDF
29	p. 32, printed p. 21). The claimed outcome: Bondarchuk coached the gold, silver, and bronze
30	medalists in hammer throw at the 1988 and other Olympic Games, "the entire Olympic podium
31	occupied by athletes of the same coach" (Bondarchuk, 1986 and 1988, as cited by Issurin).
32	
33	**Why it works: the author gives no mechanism beyond the general BPC rationale** — Issurin
34	does not describe Bondarchuk's own stated reasoning for why these particular block lengths
35	(4/4/2 weeks) were chosen. **Inference:** the entry's characterization of the three-way split
36	as organized "by competitive readiness rather than by ability type" is this entry's own
37	reading, not language Issurin uses; the mechanism Issurin offers is the same general BPC
38	logic (concentrated, sequenced blocks beat simultaneous multi-ability training) applied
39	retroactively to Bondarchuk's design.
40	
41	**When to apply: untested, use as a historical precedent, not as evidence** — Useful for
42	explaining the lineage of block-periodization thinking. Issurin presents Bondarchuk's system
43	as a parallel reform, not a source he built on: it appears in the text alongside "Issurin &
44	Kaverin, 1985, Bondarchuk, 1986, 1988" as one of the era's several reforms away from
45	traditional periodization (PDF p. 34, printed p. 23), and Issurin & Kaverin's own 1985
46	publication predates Bondarchuk's cited 1986 and 1988 works. Useful as an alternative
47	three-block naming scheme organized around competitive readiness
48	(developmental/competitive/restorative) rather than ability type
49	(accumulation/transmutation/realization); worth distinguishing the two schemes explicitly
50	when citing "Bondarchuk's blocks" versus "Issurin's blocks."
51	
52	**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — Population: elite (Olympic-level) Soviet male hammer
53	throwers training under one coach; one Olympic final's podium (plus unspecified "other
54	Olympic Games" results). This is a single coach's outcome with no comparison group, no
55	report of what other finalists' training looked like, and total reliance on the coach's and
56	Issurin's own secondary account rather than an independent case audit. A three-medal sweep at one Olympics
57	is a striking result but cannot isolate the training design's contribution from athlete
58	talent, competitor variance on the day, or other coaching factors. Do not cite this as
59	evidence that a 4/4/2-week block cadence "works" for hammer throw or any other event; it
60	illustrates a design, not a validated dose-response finding. This is distinct from and
61	should not be merged with Issurin's own accumulation/transmutation/realization taxonomy;
62	see [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]] for that separate, though
63	historically related, three-block system.
64	
65	**Example** — **Inference:** a coach citing "block periodization has a track record" should
66	specify which system (Bondarchuk's competitive-readiness blocks or Issurin's ability-type
67	blocks) and should not present the 1988 podium sweep as generalizable evidence beyond "one
68	documented historical instance this concept coincided with a strong outcome."
69	
70	**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
71	[[case-study--issurin-kaverin-canoe-kayak-block-periodization]], a comparable single-coach
72	case from the same era; consider also cross-referencing
73	`fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`

**What it is** — Issurin credits Anatoly Bondarchuk, hammer-throw coach, with one of the
precursor systems to Block Periodization (PDF p. 32, printed p. 21). Based on his own

**competitive** (load stabilizes, athletes focus on competitive performance), and
**restorative** (active recovery, preparing for the next developmental block). Stated
durations: developmental and competitive blocks are "usually four weeks," restorative "can
be shortened to two weeks." Sequencing depends on the competition schedule and individual
athlete response. The book also gives what it calls Bondarchuk's design's outstanding
characteristic: alternation and repetition of the exercise repertory in each mesocycle-block
(every four weeks); the traditional period names, preparatory, competitive, and transitory,
were kept, but Issurin notes "their essence is very different" in Bondarchuk's concept (PDF
p. 32, printed p. 21). The claimed outcome: Bondarchuk coached the gold, silver, and bronze
medalists in hammer throw at the 1988 and other Olympic Games, "the entire Olympic podium
occupied by athletes of the same coach" (Bondarchuk, 1986 and 1988, as cited by Issurin).

does not describe Bondarchuk's own stated reasoning for why these particular block lengths
(4/4/2 weeks) were chosen. **Inference:** the entry's characterization of the three-way split
as organized "by competitive readiness rather than by ability type" is this entry's own
reading, not language Issurin uses; the mechanism Issurin offers is the same general BPC
logic (concentrated, sequenced blocks beat simultaneous multi-ability training) applied
retroactively to Bondarchuk's design.

**When to apply: untested, use as a historical precedent, not as evidence** — Useful for
explaining the lineage of block-periodization thinking. Issurin presents Bondarchuk's system
as a parallel reform, not a source he built on: it appears in the text alongside "Issurin &
Kaverin, 1985, Bondarchuk, 1986, 1988" as one of the era's several reforms away from

39	of highly qualified kayakers were tracked across a full annual cycle built on the classical
40	model (Issurin et al., 1986). Measured: mean distance velocity (Vd), velocity at anaerobic
41	threshold (V-AT), peak paddle force (PF), stroke rate (SR), muscle mass (MM). Result: the
42	long general-preparatory period raised V-AT, muscle mass and peak force substantially; but
43	during the extended, highly specialized competitive period, extensive aerobic workloads were
44	replaced by more intense, event-specific exercises, and maximum-strength exercises were
45	"reduced and even rejected as harmful for racing technique" (only maximum-strength work is
46	called harmful in the source; the aerobic reduction is described as a substitution, not a
47	harm judgment), and V-AT, peak force, and muscle mass all *declined* by the competitive
48	period. Distance velocity
49	still reached its season maximum, but only via increased stroke rate compensating for
50	reduced force, i.e., technique/rate covered for a real loss in the underlying strength and
51	aerobic qualities. Issurin's summary: "the timing pattern for developing different abilities
52	was far from optimal."

54	**Why it works** — For the swimmer case, Issurin gives two separate stated mechanisms (PDF
55	p. 21, printed p. 10): extensive endurance work "captures the metabolic energy that is
56	necessary for anabolism during post-exercise recovery," which "suppresses muscle
57	hypertrophy"; and, separately, "the observations of coaches and athletes show that a
58	strenuous high volume training program causes permanent fatigue," so "the central and
59	peripheral neural factors are far from optimum." Klausen (1990) is cited for a different,
60	more general point in between the two, that enhancement of the neural mechanism "is
61	conditioned by the state of the central nervous system and the sensitivity of the
62	neuro-motor pool," not specifically for the fatigue observation. For the kayaker case, Issurin

# Two Studies Issurin Cites Against Simultaneous Development: Swimmer Interference and Kayaker Decay

**What it is** — Issurin presents two data-backed examples as motivation for abandoning
simultaneous multi-ability training (traditional periodization) in favor of consecutive,
concentrated blocks.

**(1) Swimmer concurrent-training interference (PDF pp. 21-22, printed pp. 10-11, Figure
1.3).** High-level male swimmers were studied over an 8-week early-season program combining
extensive swimming with resistive/power dry-land work aimed at swim-specific strength
(9-11 workouts/week; sample size not stated in this text). Measured: maximal force of
tethered swimming (Ftsw), dry-land explosive strength (Fexp), and dry-land strength
endurance (SE). Result: strength endurance improved markedly; swim-specific strength did not
improve; explosive strength *decreased*, despite about 30% of dry-land program time devoted
to maximal/explosive strength work. Issurin's mechanistic explanation has two separate
parts: extensive endurance work captures the metabolic energy needed for post-exercise
anabolism, which suppresses muscle hypertrophy; separately, coaches' and athletes'
observations show that a strenuous, high-volume training program causes permanent fatigue,
keeping central and peripheral neural factors far from the optimum needed for improving
muscular contraction. Klausen (1990) is cited for a more general point about what conditions
the neural mechanism (state of the CNS, sensitivity of the neuro-motor pool), not for the
fatigue observation specifically.

**(2) Kayaker decay under traditional periodization (PDF p. 25-26, printed pp. 14-15,
Figure 1.4, the in-text citation reads "Fig.1.3," which appears to be a labeling error in
the source; the described variables match Figure 1.4's caption, not Figure 1.3's).** A group
of highly qualified kayakers were tracked across a full annual cycle built on the classical
model (Issurin et al., 1986). Measured: mean distance velocity (Vd), velocity at anaerobic
threshold (V-AT), peak paddle force (PF), stroke rate (SR), muscle mass (MM). Result: the
long general-preparatory period raised V-AT, muscle mass and peak force substantially; but
during the extended, highly specialized competitive period, extensive aerobic workloads were
replaced by more intense, event-specific exercises, and maximum-strength exercises were
"reduced and even rejected as harmful for racing technique" (only maximum-strength work is
called harmful in the source; the aerobic reduction is described as a substitution, not a
harm judgment), and V-AT, peak force, and muscle mass all *declined* by the competitive
period. Distance velocity
still reached its season maximum, but only via increased stroke rate compensating for
reduced force, i.e., technique/rate covered for a real loss in the underlying strength and
aerobic qualities. Issurin's summary: "the timing pattern for developing different abilities
was far from optimal."

**Why it works** — For the swimmer case, Issurin gives two separate stated mechanisms (PDF
p. 21, printed p. 10): extensive endurance work "captures the metabolic energy that is
necessary for anabolism during post-exercise recovery," which "suppresses muscle
hypertrophy"; and, separately, "the observations of coaches and athletes show that a
strenuous high volume training program causes permanent fatigue," so "the central and
peripheral neural factors are far from optimum." Klausen (1990) is cited for a different,
more general point in between the two, that enhancement of the neural mechanism "is
conditioned by the state of the central nervous system and the sensitivity of the
neuro-motor pool," not specifically for the fatigue observation. For the kayaker case, Issurin
gives no physiological mechanism for the decline beyond narration of what happened (reduced
aerobic and strength work during the competitive period, PDF p. 25, printed p. 14); treat
that case as a described pattern, not an explained one. **Inference:** labeling the two
cases as "concurrent interference" versus "sequential decay" is this entry's own
categorization for cross-referencing purposes, not language Issurin himself uses; both are
offered by Issurin as evidence for the same underlying argument against simultaneous,
non-block training (see [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]), which in turn
motivates the consecutive block sequencing in
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]] and
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]].

**When to apply** — The swimmer study is the more detailed evidence of the two: it is an
uncontrolled, single-group, uncited 8-week observation (no control group or reference given
in this text, PDF p. 21, printed p. 10) with named outcome variables, giving concrete numbers
useful for illustrating concurrent-training interference to Baylor strength staff
programming for athletes who need both an aerobic base and explosive/max strength (e.g.,
many football positions in a fall-camp conditioning window). The kayaker case is useful
mainly as a cautionary illustration of "building a quality early in the year and then
letting it decay unaddressed."

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — The swimmer study's exact sample size is not given in
this text (only workout frequency, 9-11/week), so its statistical strength cannot be judged
from this source alone; treat the direction of the finding (interference occurred) as
`supported` but the specific numeric changes in Figure 1.3 as unverifiable: the swimmer
study carries no citation at all in this text, not even an author or year, so there is no
underlying source to check the numbers against. **Untested:** the kayaker case is Issurin's
own team's data (Issurin et al., 1986),
observational across one season with no control group; it demonstrates a plausible pattern,
not a controlled comparison against an alternative periodization model run on the same
athletes. Neither study is football-specific; football's in-season structure (weekly
competition, not one late-season peak) differs from both the swimmers' fixed 8-week block and
the kayakers' single annual peak design.

**Example** — **Inference:** a Baylor position group with both an in-season conditioning demand and a
strength-maintenance demand should treat "just add more of both" as the swimmer study's
failure mode: without deliberate sequencing or volume management, the concurrent aerobic
load can blunt the intended strength/power adaptation even when strength work is
programmed.

**Related** — [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] (Table 1.4's rationale,
which these two studies are offered as concrete illustrations of),
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]].

13	
14	# Quantifying Workout Load on a 1-5 Scale, Mapped to Borg RPE Bands
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin presents a load-related workout classification built around three
17	functions: **development**, **retention**, and **restoration** (PDF p. 52, printed p. 41).
18	Table 2.3 (PDF p. 53, printed p. 42, based on Zatsiorsky 1995, modified by Issurin 2003)
19	quantifies this on a 1-5 scale using restoration time as the objective marker: restoration
20	level 1 (< 12 hours), retention level 2 (12-24 hours), development-substantial level 3
21	(24-48 hours), development-large level 4 (48-72 hours), development-extreme level 5
22	(> 72 hours). Because restoration-time-based classification does not fit every training type
23	well (Issurin notes coordination/neuro-emotional-stress workouts need less restoration time
24	than the scale implies), Table 2.4 (PDF p. 54, printed p. 43), Issurin's own adaptation of
25	Borg's scale to workout load levels, not a direct reproduction of Borg 1973, offers a
26	parallel mapping using Borg's Rate of Perceived Exertion scale (Borg, 1973): RPE 6-11 (very-very-easy to
27	fairly-easy) = restoration; RPE 12-14 (slightly difficult) = retention; RPE 15-16
28	(difficult) = development-substantial; RPE 17-18 (very difficult) = development-large; RPE
29	19-20 (very-very difficult) = development-extreme.
30	
31	**Why it works: inference on the underlying logic** — Restoration time and perceived
32	exertion are both proxies for how disruptive a session was to homeostasis; using either (or
33	both together) lets a coach assign every workout a comparable numeric load value even in
34	non-measurable sports (team sports, gymnastics), which Issurin identifies as the practical
35	payoff: "the load level of each workout can be quantified and expressed numerically" (PDF
36	p. 54, printed p. 43), enabling load-dependent categorization (development vs. retention vs.
37	restoration) across an entire training plan, not just isolated hard/easy labeling.
38	
39	**When to apply** — Building a simple, athlete-reportable RPE-based load log for sports or
40	settings where objective physiological monitoring (HR, blood lactate) is not available for
41	every session; classifying a completed week of training after the fact into
42	development/retention/restoration proportions to check whether the intended block emphasis
43	(see [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]) was actually
44	delivered. **Eric's baseline** does not currently name Borg's RPE scale specifically, though
45	session-level subjective load tracking is philosophically consistent with the department's
46	general preference for practical, staff-sustainable monitoring tools over burdensome ones
47	(`method-baseline.md`, "Load monitoring and GPS," on why daily wellness surveys were
48	abandoned when athletes learned to game them). Session-RPE load tracking has its own gaming
49	and reliability considerations documented in team-sport settings (Comyns & Flanagan, 2013,
50	`research-papers/comyns-2013-applications-of-the-session-rating-of-perceived-exertion-system-in-professional-rugby-unio.md`;
51	McLaren et al., 2017,
52	`research-papers/mclaren-2017-a-detailed-quantification-of-differential-ratings-of-perceived-exertion-during-team-sport.md`)
53	that is not addressed anywhere in this Issurin chapter and should be treated as an open
54	question, not assumed solved.
55	
56	**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — **The author gives no mechanism** for why these
57	specific RPE cut-points (11/12, 14/15, 16/17, 18/19) map to these specific restoration-time
58	bands rather than some other set of cut-points; both tables are presented as ready-made
59	scales without a validation study cited in this chapter. RPE is a subjective, athlete-reported
60	measure and is vulnerable to the same reporting-fatigue and gaming dynamics documented
61	elsewhere for subjective wellness tools; do not treat it as equivalent in reliability to the
62	objective HR/blood-lactate markers used in Table 2.10's key-exercise prescriptions
63	(see [[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]]). The scale also does not
64	distinguish RPE driven by physical load from RPE driven by psychological/technical/cognitive

# Quantifying Workout Load on a 1-5 Scale, Mapped to Borg RPE Bands

**What it is** — Issurin presents a load-related workout classification built around three
functions: **development**, **retention**, and **restoration** (PDF p. 52, printed p. 41).
Table 2.3 (PDF p. 53, printed p. 42, based on Zatsiorsky 1995, modified by Issurin 2003)
quantifies this on a 1-5 scale using restoration time as the objective marker: restoration
level 1 (< 12 hours), retention level 2 (12-24 hours), development-substantial level 3
(24-48 hours), development-large level 4 (48-72 hours), development-extreme level 5
(> 72 hours). Because restoration-time-based classification does not fit every training type
well (Issurin notes coordination/neuro-emotional-stress workouts need less restoration time
than the scale implies), Table 2.4 (PDF p. 54, printed p. 43), Issurin's own adaptation of
Borg's scale to workout load levels, not a direct reproduction of Borg 1973, offers a
parallel mapping using Borg's Rate of Perceived Exertion scale (Borg, 1973): RPE 6-11 (very-very-easy to
fairly-easy) = restoration; RPE 12-14 (slightly difficult) = retention; RPE 15-16
(difficult) = development-substantial; RPE 17-18 (very difficult) = development-large; RPE
19-20 (very-very difficult) = development-extreme.

**Why it works: inference on the underlying logic** — Restoration time and perceived
exertion are both proxies for how disruptive a session was to homeostasis; using either (or
both together) lets a coach assign every workout a comparable numeric load value even in
non-measurable sports (team sports, gymnastics), which Issurin identifies as the practical
payoff: "the load level of each workout can be quantified and expressed numerically" (PDF
p. 54, printed p. 43), enabling load-dependent categorization (development vs. retention vs.
restoration) across an entire training plan, not just isolated hard/easy labeling.

**When to apply** — Building a simple, athlete-reportable RPE-based load log for sports or
settings where objective physiological monitoring (HR, blood lactate) is not available for
every session; classifying a completed week of training after the fact into
development/retention/restoration proportions to check whether the intended block emphasis
(see [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]) was actually
delivered. **Eric's baseline** does not currently name Borg's RPE scale specifically, though
session-level subjective load tracking is philosophically consistent with the department's
general preference for practical, staff-sustainable monitoring tools over burdensome ones
(`method-baseline.md`, "Load monitoring and GPS," on why daily wellness surveys were
abandoned when athletes learned to game them). Session-RPE load tracking has its own gaming
and reliability considerations documented in team-sport settings (Comyns & Flanagan, 2013,
`research-papers/comyns-2013-applications-of-the-session-rating-of-perceived-exertion-system-in-professional-rugby-unio.md`;
McLaren et al., 2017,
`research-papers/mclaren-2017-a-detailed-quantification-of-differential-ratings-of-perceived-exertion-during-team-sport.md`)
that is not addressed anywhere in this Issurin chapter and should be treated as an open
question, not assumed solved.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — **The author gives no mechanism** for why these
specific RPE cut-points (11/12, 14/15, 16/17, 18/19) map to these specific restoration-time
bands rather than some other set of cut-points; both tables are presented as ready-made
scales without a validation study cited in this chapter. RPE is a subjective, athlete-reported
measure and is vulnerable to the same reporting-fatigue and gaming dynamics documented
elsewhere for subjective wellness tools; do not treat it as equivalent in reliability to the
objective HR/blood-lactate markers used in Table 2.10's key-exercise prescriptions
(see [[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]]). The scale also does not
distinguish RPE driven by physical load from RPE driven by psychological/technical/cognitive
demand (e.g., a technically difficult but physically light session). Issurin notes the
restoration-time scale itself overstates load for high-level coordination training and
workouts that induce heightened neuro-emotional stress, which "usually require less time for
full restoration" than the scale would suggest (PDF p. 53, printed p. 42); this is a
comparison to the restoration-time scale, not to RPE.

**Example** — A coach without force-plate or HR-monitor access for every practice can have
players self-report session RPE and multiply by session duration, the session-RPE method
used widely in team sports (an approach not itself stated in this Issurin chapter; see
Comyns & Flanagan, 2013,
`research-papers/comyns-2013-applications-of-the-session-rating-of-perceived-exertion-system-in-professional-rugby-unio.md`,
noted here as an inference, not something Issurin describes), and classify the week's
development vs. retention vs. restoration balance against the intended training-stage
emphasis.

**Related** — [[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]],
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]].

[[research-papers/mclaren-2017-a-detailed-quantification-of-differential-ratings-of-perceived-exertion-during-team-sport]] (vault).

# Squat-First vs. Squat-After-Hang-Pull Changes Whether You Get More Reps or More Power

**What it is** — Spreuwenberg et al. (2006), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62):
**nine** resistance-trained male athletes performed the back squat (4 sets at 85% of 1RM) on
two separate days under two protocols. Protocol A: squat performed during the initial part
of the workout. Protocol B: squat performed after a whole-body resistance exercise (hang
pull). Results: Protocol A produced significantly more repetitions per set (8.0 ± 1.9 vs.
5.4 ± 2.7 in Protocol B), but average power per set was *higher* in Protocol B. The study
authors attribute (Spreuwenberg et al., 2006, as cited by Issurin) the power difference to
postactivation potentiation induced by the preceding whole-body power exercise.

**Why it works** — Issurin reports only the study authors' own attribution for the power
finding: they "attributed this phenomenon to postactivation potentiation induced by the
preceding whole-body power exercise" (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62). **Inference:** the
companion explanation for the rep-count finding, that fresh (unfatigued) muscle sustains
more total repetitions at a given relative load than muscle that has just performed a
preceding whole-body lift, is this entry's own reasoning to account for the Protocol A
result; Issurin does not state that explanation for the rep-count difference in this
passage.

**When to apply** — Choosing exercise order based on the specific training goal for that
session: Issurin's stated takeaway (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62) is that a coach wanting maximum
hypertrophy stimulus should place the squat early in the session (more total volume/reps),
while a coach targeting maximum power output should place it after appropriate whole-body
resistance work, to exploit postactivation potentiation. Directly usable for Baylor
strength-staff session design when max-effort lower-body power output (not volume) is the
stated goal of a given lift.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — This is a small (n = 9), single published study;
Issurin does not report effect sizes, statistical significance values, or the specific
whole-body exercise's loading in this citation beyond "hang pull"; treat the direction of
the finding as `supported` but do not treat the exact magnitude (8.0 vs. 5.4 reps) as
something to replicate precisely without reading the original study. It is unclear from this
text whether the postactivation-potentiation effect generalizes to different athlete
populations (this sample was resistance-trained males), different preceding exercises, or
different rest intervals between the potentiating exercise and the squat.

**Example** — **Inference:** a power-focused lower-body day for football linemen might
sequence a moderate-load hang pull or clean pull before back squats at 85% 1RM, accepting
fewer total squat reps in exchange for higher power output per rep on the squats that
follow; a hypertrophy-focused day for the same lift would instead put the squat first.

**Related** — [[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]],
[[research-papers/hanson-2007-acute-effects-of-heavy-and-light-load-squat-exercise-on-the-kinetic-measures-of-vertical-j]] (vault),
[[research-papers/hirayama-2014-acute-effects-of-an-ascending-intensity-squat-protocol-on-vertical-jump-performance]] (vault),
[[research-papers/seitz-2017-a-sled-push-stimulus-potentiates-subsequent-20-m-sprint-performance]] (vault).

# A Structured Warm-Up/Cool-Down Program Cut Soccer Injuries Roughly Four-Fold Over Six Months

**What it is** — Ekstrand et al. (1983), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 58, printed p. 47,
Figure 2.1): **twelve** national-division soccer teams (**180 players**) were split into two
groups. The intervention group (six teams) used a modified program with carefully structured
warm-ups (ball exercises plus a stretching program) and cool-downs (jogging plus hold-relax
stretching), supervised by doctors and physiotherapists. The control group (six teams)
trained traditionally. Over a six-month follow-up, the intervention group showed "highly
significant superiority": a roughly **four-fold reduction in the number of injuries** and a
"drastic decrease" in workouts and games missed to musculoskeletal disorders. Issurin
separately cites supporting single-factor findings: stretching in warm-up increases lower
extremity range of motion in soccer players (Moller et al., 1985); active warm-up *without*
stretching does not affect flexibility (Zakas et al., 2006); and intense prior exercise
meaningfully stimulates aerobic metabolism in working muscles during subsequent strenuous
performance (Bangsbo et al., 2001). A related study (Moller et al., 1985, PDF p. 68, printed
p. 57) tracked 48 adult soccer players across three warm-up/cool-down protocols. The regular
soccer workout (no stretching) caused a significant decrease in all range-of-motion (ROM)
indices. A similar workout with a stretching series in the *warm-up* produced more favorable
ROM responses immediately after the session, with 24-hour ROM not reported for that arm. The
third version, with the stretching series inserted in the *cool-down*, produced significant
ROM benefits both immediately after the workout and 24 hours later.

**Why it works** — Issurin gives warm-up three stated functions: metabolic adjustment,
technical/coordination adjustment, and attainment of mental readiness (Table 2.6, PDF p. 60,
printed p. 49). Cool-down gets four stated objectives, given in prose rather than a table:
reduce body temperature, heart rate, and blood pressure to resting levels; remove acid
metabolites and other waste products from the muscles to the circulatory system for further
clearance; facilitate recovery of the endocrine system; and reduce emotional tension and
support positive mental recovery (PDF p. 67, printed p. 56).

**Contested, terminology only:** Issurin's cool-down rationale frames blood lactate and
"other acid metabolites" as "waste products" to be "removed" from the muscles (PDF pp.
67-69, printed pp. 56-58), and separately states that slow locomotion "causes faster lactate
removal" (Bonen & Belcastro, 1976, PDF p. 68, printed p. 57), with blood lactate removal
after a 4-minute exhausting time trial taking about 20 minutes of restoration (Juel et al.,
1990, PDF p. 70, printed p. 59). The vault's Verkhoshansky staging entry
([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths]], `proven`) treats
lactate as a normal metabolic byproduct and fuel source, not a toxin, and states that blood
lactate returns to normal within about an hour of strenuous interval training; its `proven`
rating is scoped to two corrections, that lactate is not the cause of DOMS and that "oxygen
debt" is better described as recovery oxygen consumption. That entry does not say clearance
happens "regardless of cool-down activity"; that claim belongs to neither source and should
not be attributed to either. The two books' clearance-time figures are consistent with each
other (about 20 minutes after a 4-minute trial vs. within about an hour of a strenuous
interval session), and neither source ties lactate to DOMS: Issurin attributes DOMS to
strong eccentric ("plyometric") work instead (PDF pp. 69-70, printed pp. 58-59). The real
disagreement is terminology: Issurin's "acid metabolites and other waste products" (PDF p.
67, printed p. 56) against the Verkhoshansky entry's "normal byproduct and fuel." Keep this
book's clearance-time number and its active-recovery claim (slow locomotion speeds lactate
removal); do not repeat "waste product" as physiology, and do not attribute a "toxin" claim
or a "regardless of cool-down activity" claim to Issurin, since he states neither.

**When to apply** — The Ekstrand et al. (1983) result is directly relevant to Applied
Performance's collaboration with Athletic Medicine on injury reduction: a structured,
medically-supervised warm-up/cool-down protocol is associated with a large, measured
reduction in soft-tissue injury incidence in a team sport, over a real six-month season, not
an acute lab measure. The cool-down-stretching timing finding (Moller et al., 1985) suggests
cool-down, not just warm-up, is where a stretching series may do more for next-day range of
motion.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — This is a controlled team-level trial (6 intervention
teams vs. 6 control teams; the method of allocating teams to condition is not described),
and the intervention bundled multiple changes at once (warm-up content, cool-down content,

# A Structured Warm-Up/Cool-Down Program Cut Soccer Injuries Roughly Four-Fold Over Six Months

**What it is** — Ekstrand et al. (1983), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 58, printed p. 47,
Figure 2.1): **twelve** national-division soccer teams (**180 players**) were split into two
groups. The intervention group (six teams) used a modified program with carefully structured
warm-ups (ball exercises plus a stretching program) and cool-downs (jogging plus hold-relax
stretching), supervised by doctors and physiotherapists. The control group (six teams)
trained traditionally. Over a six-month follow-up, the intervention group showed "highly
significant superiority": a roughly **four-fold reduction in the number of injuries** and a
"drastic decrease" in workouts and games missed to musculoskeletal disorders. Issurin
separately cites supporting single-factor findings: stretching in warm-up increases lower
extremity range of motion in soccer players (Moller et al., 1985); active warm-up *without*
stretching does not affect flexibility (Zakas et al., 2006); and intense prior exercise
meaningfully stimulates aerobic metabolism in working muscles during subsequent strenuous
performance (Bangsbo et al., 2001). A related study (Moller et al., 1985, PDF p. 68, printed
p. 57) tracked 48 adult soccer players across three warm-up/cool-down protocols. The regular
soccer workout (no stretching) caused a significant decrease in all range-of-motion (ROM)
indices. A similar workout with a stretching series in the *warm-up* produced more favorable
ROM responses immediately after the session, with 24-hour ROM not reported for that arm. The
third version, with the stretching series inserted in the *cool-down*, produced significant
ROM benefits both immediately after the workout and 24 hours later.

**Why it works** — Issurin gives warm-up three stated functions: metabolic adjustment,
technical/coordination adjustment, and attainment of mental readiness (Table 2.6, PDF p. 60,
printed p. 49). Cool-down gets four stated objectives, given in prose rather than a table:
reduce body temperature, heart rate, and blood pressure to resting levels; remove acid
metabolites and other waste products from the muscles to the circulatory system for further
clearance; facilitate recovery of the endocrine system; and reduce emotional tension and
support positive mental recovery (PDF p. 67, printed p. 56).

**Contested, terminology only:** Issurin's cool-down rationale frames blood lactate and
"other acid metabolites" as "waste products" to be "removed" from the muscles (PDF pp.
67-69, printed pp. 56-58), and separately states that slow locomotion "causes faster lactate
removal" (Bonen & Belcastro, 1976, PDF p. 68, printed p. 57), with blood lactate removal
after a 4-minute exhausting time trial taking about 20 minutes of restoration (Juel et al.,
1990, PDF p. 70, printed p. 59). The vault's Verkhoshansky staging entry
([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths]], `proven`) treats
lactate as a normal metabolic byproduct and fuel source, not a toxin, and states that blood
lactate returns to normal within about an hour of strenuous interval training; its `proven`
rating is scoped to two corrections, that lactate is not the cause of DOMS and that "oxygen
debt" is better described as recovery oxygen consumption. That entry does not say clearance
happens "regardless of cool-down activity"; that claim belongs to neither source and should
not be attributed to either. The two books' clearance-time figures are consistent with each
other (about 20 minutes after a 4-minute trial vs. within about an hour of a strenuous
interval session), and neither source ties lactate to DOMS: Issurin attributes DOMS to
strong eccentric ("plyometric") work instead (PDF pp. 69-70, printed pp. 58-59). The real
disagreement is terminology: Issurin's "acid metabolites and other waste products" (PDF p.
67, printed p. 56) against the Verkhoshansky entry's "normal byproduct and fuel." Keep this
book's clearance-time number and its active-recovery claim (slow locomotion speeds lactate
removal); do not repeat "waste product" as physiology, and do not attribute a "toxin" claim
or a "regardless of cool-down activity" claim to Issurin, since he states neither.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** the Ekstrand et al. (1983) result is directly relevant to
Applied Performance's collaboration with Athletic Medicine on injury reduction: a structured,
medically-supervised warm-up/cool-down protocol is associated with a large, measured
reduction in soft-tissue injury incidence in a team sport, over a real six-month season, not
an acute lab measure. The cool-down-stretching timing finding (Moller et al., 1985) suggests
cool-down, not just warm-up, is where a stretching series may do more for next-day range of
motion.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — This is a controlled team-level trial (6 intervention
teams vs. 6 control teams; the method of allocating teams to condition is not described),
and the intervention bundled multiple changes at once (warm-up content, cool-down content,
and medical/physiotherapy supervision), so the four-fold injury reduction cannot be
attributed to warm-up or cool-down alone: Issurin himself flags this study as "atypical
because it refers to the complex effects of warming-up, cooling-down and medical supervision"
(PDF p. 58, printed p. 47). **Contested:** stretching's effect on preventing delayed-onset
muscle soreness specifically is described by Issurin himself as disputed within this same
chapter, "supported by several studies (Hartfield, 1985) and contradicted by others (High
et al., 1989)" (PDF p. 70, printed p. 59); do not cite stretching-prevents-DOMS as settled.

**Example** — **Inference:** a Baylor position group's practice-ending routine that pairs light locomotion
with a stretching series (rather than stretching only in the pre-practice warm-up) has some
support here for next-day range-of-motion benefit, though the causal strength of the
underlying Moller et al. (1985) study for injury outcomes specifically (as opposed to ROM)
is not established by this citation.

# Which Training Modalities Tolerate Fatigue, and Which Need a Fresh Athlete

**What it is** — Figure 2.3 (PDF p. 71, printed p. 60) ranks twelve training modalities by
how much athlete fatigue they can tolerate before the acute training effect is compromised,
from "well rested" through "slightly fatigued," "moderately fatigued," to "fatigued":
**well rested only**: maximal speed (least fatigue-tolerant of all); **well rested to
slightly fatigued**: maximal strength (neural mechanism, e.g. 1-3RM), explosive strength,
acquisition of new technical skills, anaerobic glycolytic power; **up to moderately
fatigued**: anaerobic glycolytic capacity, aerobic power, maximal strength (hypertrophy,
e.g. 8-10RM); **through to fatigued, end of session (most fatigue-tolerant)**: aerobic
endurance (long duration), strength endurance, technique perfection, flexibility. Issurin's
stated reasoning (PDF pp. 71-73, printed pp. 60-62): exercises needing precise excitatory
neural output (max speed, explosive strength, technical skill acquisition, neural-mechanism
strength) are blocked by inhibitory CNS output in fatigued athletes, so they belong early;
anaerobic glycolytic power needs available energy reserves that are depleted in fatigued
athletes; aerobic power's acute effect depends on the total duration of exercise performed
close to maximum oxygen uptake, a metabolic level moderately fatigued athletes can still
sustain (PDF p. 72, printed p. 61); hypertrophy-strength work depends on total mechanical
work and post-exercise recovery conditions, not the athlete's pre-exercise freshness, so it
can be placed later, even after an endurance session; anaerobic glycolytic capacity,
technique perfection, and strength/aerobic endurance work are defined by sustained effort
*despite* accumulating fatigue ("some part of technique perfection can be performed by
fatigued athletes," PDF p. 73, printed p. 62), so some fatigue is expected and even required
for the intended stimulus.

**Why it works** — CNS-dependent, high-precision, high-velocity qualities are limited by
inhibitory neural output and available energy stores that both degrade with fatigue, while
volume/duration-dependent qualities (hypertrophy, strength/aerobic endurance, technique
perfection late in a session) depend on total accumulated work or post-session recovery
rather than the athlete's moment-to-moment freshness. Sequencing exists to protect the
fatigue-sensitive qualities' window, not because "harder exercises always go first."

**When to apply** — Ordering exercises within a single practice or lift: place max-speed
work, new skill acquisition, explosive strength, and low-rep neural-strength work at the
start of a session (or after only light warm-up fatigue); place hypertrophy work, technical
perfection under fatigue, and long-duration aerobic/strength-endurance work later, when some
accumulated fatigue is acceptable or even intended. Issurin gives a worked example (PDF
p. 72, printed p. 61): an endurance athlete needing to preserve muscle mass can have a
hypertrophy-focused strength session (8-10RM) placed *after* a medium-load endurance
session, because hypertrophy's driver is total mechanical work and post-workout recovery
conditions, not pre-workout freshness; this would be the wrong sequencing choice for a
neural-strength (1-3RM) session, which does need "prime time."

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — The author gives no primary citation for Figure 2.3
itself: it reads as the author's own synthesized ranking rather than a reproduced,
independently-sourced scale; treat the ordinal ranking (which modality is more or less
fatigue-tolerant than its neighbor) as a reasonable but unvalidated synthesis, not a measured
result. The figure gives no guidance on *how much* fatigue is "slight" vs. "moderate" in
objective terms (RPE, HR, or specific fatigue markers), so applying it requires a coach's own
judgment call about where an athlete currently sits on that continuum. It also does not
address multi-session days directly: see [[heuristic--two-a-day-workout-sequencing-by-dominant-ability]]
for cross-session sequencing.

**Example** — **Inference:** a football practice combining new install (technical skill
acquisition) with conditioning: install work belongs at the start of practice when players
are fresh and can attend to technical detail; conditioning work belongs at the end, where
sustained effort under fatigue is the intended stimulus rather than a limitation.

# No More Than Three Training Modalities Per Workout, With 65-70% of Time on One or Two

**What it is** — Issurin extends the concentration principle to single-session design
(Figure 2.4, PDF p. 74, printed p. 63; Table 2.12, PDF p. 76, printed p. 65) with five
stated rules (PDF p. 75, printed p. 64): (1) a workout should contain **no more than three
training modalities**, typically one dominant, one compatible with the main purpose, and
one for technique/tactics improvement or restoration; (2) **65-70% of total training time**
in a development workout should go to one or two selected modalities, to preserve workload
concentration; (3) the typical frequency of workouts in high-performance training (6-12 a
week) dictates certain conditions for the session after a key-workout: it should show a
significant load reduction, and running two consecutive key-workouts, while possible, risks
excessive load concentration; (4) hypertrophy-focused sessions require workload to be
"substantially reduced" for **at least 20 hours** afterward to protect the anabolic phase of
muscle restoration; (5) limiting modality count matters most in high-performance sport; the
daily program for juniors, for example, may be more diverse, multilateral, and therefore
more attractive. Figure 2.4 maps which modalities are compatible as secondary/tertiary
additions to five dominant ones: aerobic endurance pairs with alactic sprint,
strength-endurance-aerobic, and hypertrophy-strength (placed after); anaerobic glycolytic
endurance pairs with strength-endurance-anaerobic, aerobic restoration, and mixed
aerobic-anaerobic endurance; alactic sprint pairs with aerobic endurance, explosive
strength, hypertrophy-strength (after), and aerobic restoration; hypertrophy-strength pairs
with neural-strength, flexibility, and aerobic restoration; and, when learning new technical
elements is the dominant task, any kind of training modality may be added, but only *after*
the dominant, technical-learning task, not before it. Table 2.12 gives the
physiological/psychological rationale for
several of the strongest pairings (e.g., aerobic endurance + strength endurance: increased
oxidation supports the resistance work; alactic sprint + aerobic endurance: brief sprints
break monotony and keep a wide muscle-fiber pool activated for the subsequent aerobic work).

**Why it works: the specific numeric thresholds are asserted, not derived** — The
underlying logic is the same concentration principle from Chapter 1
([[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]): splitting a session across too many
modalities dilutes the stimulus for all of them. **Inference:** Issurin gives no stated
derivation for why the cutoff is exactly three modalities rather than two or four, why the
time-share threshold is 65-70% rather than some other range, or why 20 hours is the specific
reduced-load window after hypertrophy work (versus, e.g., 24 or 48 hours); these read as
the author's own practical rules of thumb built from coaching experience rather than
citations to a dose-response study.

**When to apply** — Auditing whether a practice plan or lift is trying to do too much:
count distinct training modalities in a session and check whether one or two of them
actually receive the majority of training time, per the 65-70% rule. Use Figure 2.4/Table
2.12 to check whether a planned secondary modality is a known-compatible pairing or an
unaddressed combination. **Eric's baseline:** the class-1 lecture (transcript pp.28-29)
presents this same Figure 2.4 chart, and the course attributes its block-periodization
material to Issurin (week1-lecture.md marker p.64); "incompatible qualities... are not both
targeted at full intensity in the same block" (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and
programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.28-29, "you can't ride two
horses with one saddle") is the same instinct at the block level rather than the
single-session level. This Issurin entry gives that instinct a specific numeric structure
(≤3 modalities, 65-70% time-share) that the baseline material does not itself repeat at the
session level.

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — Treat the ≤3-modality, 65-70%, and 20-hour figures as
Issurin's own heuristics rather than established constants: no citation or underlying data
is given for any of the three in this chapter. Issurin explicitly narrows the number
constraints to high-performance training; junior/developmental programming is stated to
reasonably need more variety, not fewer modalities. Figure 2.4's compatibility map is not
exhaustive (it covers five dominant modalities, not every possible combination); an
untested pairing should not be assumed incompatible or compatible by default; Issurin gives
no guidance for modalities not shown in the figure.

**Example** — **Inference:** a practice plan combining strength-endurance, aerobic-anaerobic
conditioning, maximal-speed sprint work, and new-install technical work in one session would
have four distinct modalities, exceeding the stated ≤3 rule. Per Figure 2.4, glycolytic
endurance pairs well with strength-endurance-anaerobic and aerobic restoration; new-install
technical work, if it is the priority for the day, should stay the dominant, first task of
its own session (per Figure 2.3, new-skill acquisition needs a well-rested or only slightly
fatigued athlete), with strength-endurance or conditioning work added afterward, or moved to
a separate session entirely, rather than demoted to a secondary slot after glycolytic work.

**Related** — [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]],
[[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
[[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]].

# A Morning Full-Body Resistance Workout Did Not Hurt Jump, Anaerobic Power, or Shooting Accuracy Six Hours Later

**What it is** — Woolstenhulme et al. (2004), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 80, printed p. 69):
highly trained female basketball players (ages 18-22; exact sample size not stated in this
text) completed a within-subject comparison on two separate days. On the experimental day,
they performed a full-body morning resistance workout (7 exercises, 3-6 sets, 5-12RM loads),
then after **six hours of rest** were tested on vertical jump, a 30-second Wingate anaerobic
cycling test, and a 60-second shooting-accuracy trial. On the control day, the same test
battery was completed without the preceding resistance workout. Statistical analysis found
no differences between the athletes' results on the experimental vs. control days. Issurin's
stated conclusion: "a high-resistance full-body workout of moderate intensity has no negative
impact on the manifestation of sport-specific athletic abilities of trained basketball
players after six hours of rest."

**Why it works: inference, not stated in the cited passage** — Six hours appears to be
sufficient for the acute neuromuscular fatigue from a moderate-intensity, moderate-volume
resistance session (5-12RM, 7 exercises) to resolve enough that it does not measurably
degrade jump, anaerobic power, or a skill-accuracy task; Issurin does not present the
physiological recovery mechanism in this passage beyond citing the outcome.

**When to apply** — Issurin frames this as an additional comment on sequencing resistance
workouts and game practice "in dual and team sports," where "regular strength training is an
indispensable part of in-season preparation on professional and semi-professional teams"
(PDF p. 79, printed p. 68); he does not name football specifically. **Inference:** this
applies to football, a team sport with a long competitive season, for the same practical
question: whether morning hours can be used for resistance training on a day with afternoon
practice or competition, given that in-season strength training is described elsewhere in this chapter as necessary
to offset the "dramatic losses of lean body mass, and maximum and explosive strength" a long
20-35 week competitive season can otherwise cause (Baker, 2001; Gamble, 2006, as cited by
Issurin, PDF pp. 79-80). This gives a specific, citable data point (six hours, moderate
5-12RM loading) supporting a same-day AM-lift/PM-practice-or-game model, consistent with
Eric's baseline's general in-season rule to "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than
avoid lifting in-season (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.20-21).

**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — The cited sample is female basketball players; exact
sample size, loading specifics beyond "5-12RM," and effect-size/statistical detail are not
given in this text, so the finding should be treated as a directional result, not a precise
dosing guarantee. **Inference:** football involves substantially higher-impact,
higher-volume, and often heavier absolute loading than a 5-12RM "moderate intensity"
basketball-focused protocol, and involves collision-based rather than jump/shoot-accuracy
outcome measures; do not assume this six-hour window transfers unchanged to a heavier
football-specific lift or to contact-sport performance measures without independent
verification. The study also does not address multi-day accumulated fatigue from repeated
same-day lift-then-compete scheduling across a full season, only a single isolated
comparison day.

**Example** — **Inference:** a football program considering morning lifts on game day or heavy-practice
days has a citable data point that a moderate-intensity, moderate-volume full-body session
six hours before performance testing did not degrade jump, anaerobic power, or a
skill-accuracy measure in one studied population, but should treat football-specific
validation (heavier loads, contact-sport outcome measures) as a separate, unanswered
question.

**Related** — [[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]],
[[heuristic--two-a-day-workout-sequencing-by-dominant-ability]].

content.content:
`case-study--issurin-kaverin-canoe-kayak-block-periodization.md` | Changed "the author and colleagues judged excessive" to the book's actual wording, "the prevailing opinion was that this load level was excessive" (confirmed against the page image); added the 4/4/2-week durations and their "physiological and biochemical prerequisites" rationale; relabeled "reporting on his own uncontrolled intervention with his own national team" as an Inference, since the book states the Issurin & Kaverin 1985 publication but not Issurin's personal role; em-dash cleanup.

`framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept.md` | Fixed Table 2.10 locator to PDF 66/printed 55; added the missing "lactate 1-2.5" to the restoration row; labeled the monitoring-feasibility clause and the ODSF baseline analogy Inference; labeled the Example Inference; em-dash cleanup.

`framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping.md` | Rewrote the restoration-scale nuance to compare against the restoration-time scale (as the book does) rather than RPE; added "(Issurin's own adaptation of Borg's scale, not a direct reproduction of Borg 1973)" to Table 2.4; replaced the uncited "well-documented gaming risk" and "standard extension of Borg RPE elsewhere in sport science" claims with named citations (Comyns & Flanagan 2013, McLaren et al. 2017, both in the vault) per G3; added reciprocal-link suggestions to those two vault entries in Related.

`claim--morning-resistance-training-no-decrement-after-6hr-rest.md` | Corrected "per Issurin's framing" to his actual framing, "dual and team sports" and "professional and semi-professional teams" (PDF 79/printed 68, confirmed against the page image), not football by name; added an explicit Inference for the football application; labeled the Example Inference.

`case-study--postactivation-potentiation-exercise-order-squat-study.md` | Changed "Issurin attributes" to "the study authors attribute (Spreuwenberg et al., 2006, as cited by Issurin)," since the book attributes the finding to the study's own authors, not to Issurin (confirmed against the page image); labeled the Example Inference; added the three suggested PAP Related links (hanson-2007, hirayama-2014, seitz-2017, all in the vault).

`case-study--warmup-cooldown-injury-reduction-soccer.md` | Rewrote the lactate contest as terminology-only: removed the "toxin" and "regardless of cool-down activity" claims (neither source makes them), added Issurin's active-recovery citation (Bonen & Belcastro 1976) and the correct Juel et al. 1990 locator (PDF 70/printed 59, not 57-58), and stated plainly that neither source ties lactate to DOMS (Issurin attributes DOMS to eccentric work); fixed "three functions each" to warm-up's three functions versus cool-down's four objectives, sourced from the correct prose location (PDF 67/printed 56, not Table 2.11); replaced "observational, non-randomized" with "controlled team-level trial (6 vs 6 teams, allocation method not described)"; fixed the Moller et al. 1985 study description (regular workout caused a significant ROM decrease; warm-up-only stretching was favorable immediately after with 24h not reported for that arm); labeled the Example Inference; updated the reciprocal-link note.

`heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state.md` | Fixed Figure 2.3 locator to PDF 71/printed 60 and the modality count to twelve; replaced the fatigue-tolerance groupings with the corrected four bands (well rested: maximal speed only; well rested to slightly fatigued: neural-strength, explosive strength, new-technical-skill acquisition, anaerobic glycolytic power; up to moderately fatigued: anaerobic glycolytic capacity, aerobic power, hypertrophy-strength; through to fatigued: aerobic endurance, strength endurance, technique perfection, flexibility), all confirmed against the page image bar lengths; added the aerobic-power rationale (PDF 72/printed 61); labeled the Example Inference; em-dash cleanup.

`heuristic--two-a-day-workout-sequencing-by-dominant-ability.md` | Fixed "up to four (routine in training-camp practice)" to the book's actual claim (two- and three-workout days routine; four-to-six anecdotal, six exceptional); replaced the Figure 2.5 session-content paragraph with the correct S1-S4 table (confirmed against the page image: the entry had shifted alactic/aerobic content by one session); added the source inconsistency Issurin flags himself between Figure 2.6's session-2 label and its body-text description; labeled the football fall-camp application Inference and added the NCAA/Baylor-schedule check; added the book's stated purpose for subdividing daily training (PDF 77/printed 66) to Why it works, labeling the break-length generalization Inference; labeled the Example Inference; em-dash cleanup.

## Summary

17 of 17 review rows applied (16 entries + `_book.md`). 0 not applied. 0 disagreements with the review; every locator and quote the review specified was independently re-verified against the source PDF page image and matched. Global fixes G1-G5 applied library-wide across all 16 Ch1-2 entries: unlabeled invented Examples/applications now carry "Inference:" (except the two rows the review names as already-fine: the Bondarchuk-lineage caution in `case-study--issurin-kaverin-canoe-kayak-block-periodization.md`'s Example, and the sRPE-times-duration clause in `framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping.md`'s Example); body-prose em dashes replaced with commas, colons, or semicolons (all 16 files now carry exactly 6 em dashes, all in the house-style "**Header** — text" position, matching the Moyer reference file's count); uncited "well-documented"/"standard extension" claims now cite a named paper or were removed; the Issurin 2016 vault brief is now linked and cited by page wherever the book's confident framing needed qualifying; "independently arrived at"/"converges" claims about Eric's baseline now state the course teaches this material directly from Issurin (week1-lecture.md, the class-1 transcript), confirmed by grep against those source files.
